en: The Chapter on Conduct (Ācārādhyāya)
Having honored Yājñavalkya, the lord of yogis, the sages said:
"Tell us in their entirety the duties of those belonging to the castes and stages of life, as well as others."
Remaining in Mithilā, that lord of yogis, having meditated thoroughly, spoke to the sages:
"In whatever region there is a black antelope, there you should learn the dharmas. (1.2)
The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, and the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) of the Vedas—these fourteen are the seats of knowledge and of dharma. 1.3.
The exponents of the Dharmaśāstras are Manu, Viṣṇu, Yama, Aṅgiras, Vasiṣṭha, Dakṣa, Saṃvarta, Śātātapa, and Parāśara. (1.4)
Āpastamba, Uśanas, Vyāsa, Kātyāyana, Bṛhaspati, Gautama, Śaṅkha and Likhita, Hārīta, Atri, and likewise I [Yājñavalkya]. (1.5)
Whatever substance is given to a worthy recipient by those endowed with faith, through the proper place, time, and means— that is the complete definition of dharma.
The Veda, the Smṛti, the conduct of the virtuous, and what is pleasing to oneself—desire born of a pure resolve: this is remembered as the root of Dharma. ||1.7||
Of the acts of sacrifice, ritual conduct, self-restraint, non-violence, charity, and the study of sacred texts—this indeed is the supreme dharma: the perception of the Self through yoga. 1.8.

An assembly of four who know the Vedic law, or even one consisting of those learned in the three Vedas—whatever such an assembly declares shall be the Dharma; or else, a single person who is the most excellent among those who know the inner self. 1.9.
The castes are the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras; however, the first three are the twice-born.
For them, the rites beginning with the impregnation and ending with the funeral ground are indeed performed with sacred mantras.

The rite of conception (garbhādhāna) should be performed during the fertile period; the rite of male-conception (pumsavana) before the fetus moves; the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) in the sixth or eighth month; and these [rites], along with the birth-rite (jātakarman), are to be performed at the time of birth. 1.11.
On the eleventh day the naming ceremony is performed; in the fourth month the first outing;
in the sixth month the first feeding of solid food; and the tonsure ceremony should be carried out according to family custom.
In this way, the sin arising from seed and womb is pacified;
these rites for women are performed silently, but the marriage ceremony is accompanied by mantras.

The initiation ceremony (upanayana) for a Brāhmaṇa should take place in the eighth year from conception or in the eighth year [from birth]; for Kṣatriyas, in the eleventh year plus one; for Vaiśyas, in the twelfth year, or according to family custom. 1.14.

Having initiated the pupil with the Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛti) as a preliminary, the teacher should subsequently teach him the Veda and instruct him in the rules of purification and conduct. ||1.15||
During the day and at the twilights, with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) placed over the ear, one should void urine and feces facing north; however, if it is at night, one should face south. 1.16.
Having risen with his penis still held [in the hand], he should untiringly perform purification with earth and drawn-up water, effecting the removal of odor and residue. 1.17.
Seated with his knees together in a clean place, facing either north or east, a twice-born man should always perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma-tīrtha. 1.18.
The bases of the little finger, the forefinger, and the thumb, as well as the tip of the hand, are respectively the *prājāpatya*, *pitrya*, *brāhma*, and *daivata* tirthas. (1.19)

Having sipped water three times and wiped [the mouth] twice, one should touch the cavities and the upper part [of the body]; [this should be done] with water that is natural, free from foam and bubbles. (1.20)
The twice-born classes are purified by water reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate respectively; a woman and a Śūdra are purified by water touched once at the end [of the mouth]. (1.21)
Bathing with mantras dedicated to the water-deities, sprinkling [the body], restraint of the breath, worship of the sun, and the daily recitation of the Gāyatrī. ||1.22||
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with its head (śiras) preceded by the Vyāhṛtis and joined with each Praṇava; this is the threefold restraint of breath (prāṇasaṃyama). 1.23.
Having restrained his breath and become purified, he should sit reciting the Sāvitrī with the three verses addressed to the waters until the stars appear.
One should thus stand during the morning twilight facing the east until the sun appears;
then one should perform the fire-rite during both twilights.
Then he should salute his elders, saying, "I am so-and-so," and he should also attend upon his teacher with a concentrated mind for the sake of Vedic study. 1.26.
When summoned, he should study; whatever he has received, he should announce it to him;
and he should always act for his benefit through the deeds of mind, speech, and body. (1.27)

Those who are grateful, non-malicious, intelligent, pure, of noble birth, and free from envy; who are virtuous, capable, trustworthy, and provide for their own needs—these, according to dharma, are the ones to be taught. 1.28.
He should carry a staff, a deerskin, a sacred thread, and a girdle;
he should go about for alms among blameless Brahmins for the sake of his own subsistence. (1.29)
The practice of begging for alms by Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas is characterized by the word "bhava" at its beginning, middle, and end, respectively. (1.30)
Established in the life of a student, a Brahmin shall not eat food from a single source except in times of distress;
however, he may eat at a śrāddha feast at his pleasure, provided it does not cause him to violate his vow.
One should avoid honey, meat, collyrium, leavings of food, fermented acids, women, and the harming of living beings; one should also avoid looking at the sun, foul language, and slander. 1.32.
He is a *guru* who, having performed the rites, imparts the Veda to him; he who initiates him and gives him the Veda is called an *ācārya*. (1.33)
The teacher who imparts even a single portion [of knowledge] is called an *upādhyāya*, and the one who performs the sacrifice is called an *ṛtvij*.
These are to be honored according to their precedence; yet among them all, the mother is the most venerable. (1.34)
Having performed his fire-ritual, he should eat while maintaining silence, with the permission of his teacher;
preceded by the ritual of *apośāna*, he should honor the food and not disparage it. (1.35)
For each Veda, the period of studentship (brahmacarya) shall last twelve years or five;
some say it lasts until the Veda has been mastered, and the tonsure ceremony (keśānta) takes place in the sixteenth year.
The time for the initiation ceremony for the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas extends beyond the sixteenth, the twenty-second, and the twenty-fourth year respectively. (1.37)
From this point forward, these people fall, excluded from all religious duties;
they are outcasts from the Sāvitrī, becoming Vratyas, except through the Vratyastoma sacrifice.

The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are born once before [the ceremony] from their mother, and a second time at the binding of the girdle of Muñja grass; therefore, these are called "twice-born. (1.39)
For the twice-born, the Veda alone is the supreme means for attaining the highest good, whether through sacrifices, austerities, or auspicious deeds. 1.40.
That twice-born man who studies the Rigvedic verses every day shall satisfy the gods with honey and milk, and the ancestors with honey and clarified butter.
He who studies the Yajus formulas every day according to his ability gratifies the gods with ghee and nectar,
and likewise the ancestors with clarified butter and honey.
He who recites this daily shall satisfy the gods with Soma and clarified butter;
and he shall provide satisfaction for the ancestors with honey and ghee.
Reciting the Atharva-Angiras hymns, the twice-born man should satisfy the gods with fat, and the ancestors daily with honey and clarified butter, according to his ability. (1.44)
He who studies daily, according to his ability, the dialogues (vākovākya), the Purāṇas, the Nārāśaṃsīs, the Gāthās, the Itihāsas, and the sciences (vidyā). || 1.45 ||
He provides the gods with a satiating offering of meat, milk-rice,
and honey, and likewise satisfies the ancestors with honey and clarified butter.
Satisfied themselves, they satisfy him with the auspicious fruits of all his desires;
whatever sacrifice he studies, he shall obtain the fruit of each one.

The twice-born who constantly engages in the private recitation of the Veda (svādhyāya) here on earth enjoys the fruit of three gifts of the earth filled with wealth, as well as that of supreme austerity.
But a lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) shall dwell in the presence of his teacher; in the absence of the teacher, in his son, in his wife, or even in the sacred fire (vaiśvānara). 1.49.
Practicing this method with his senses conquered, he attains the world of Brahmā and is not born here again. ||1.50||
Having given a gift to his teacher, he should bathe with his permission,
whether he has mastered the Veda, or the vows, or both.

Having remained chaste, he should marry a woman endowed with auspicious marks—one who has belonged to no other man before, who is pleasing to him, who is not a sapinda relative, and who is younger than himself. (1.52)

One who is healthy, has brothers, and is not born of the same lineage (gotra) or from the same sage (ṛṣi); likewise, she should be the fifth or seventh in descent from the mother's side and the father's side.
From a great family of Vedic scholars renowned for ten generations, even if it be prosperous, yet not afflicted by the defect of hereditary diseases. (1.54)
A bridegroom of the same caste who possesses these very qualities, who is learned in the Vedas, carefully tested for virility, young, wise, and beloved by the people, is the best choice. (1.55)
As for what is said regarding the taking of a wife from a Śūdra by those of the twice-born castes—that is not my opinion, because in that case, he himself is born [from her]. (1.56)
Three wives in the order of the castes, likewise two, and one respectively, are the own wives for the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya; [one] for the one born as a Śūdra. 1.57.
The Brāhma marriage is that in which [the bride] is invited and given, adorned according to one's ability;
the son born of it purifies twenty-one persons on both sides. 1.58.
The *daiva* marriage is one where the bridegroom gives a cow and a bull to the officiating priest at the sacrifice; the *ārṣa* marriage consists of giving two cows.
The son born of the first [the *daiva*] purifies fourteen generations, and the son born of the latter [the *ārṣa*] purifies six.
When it is given to a seeker with the words, "Let the Dharma be practiced together," that primary body purifies six ancestors, six descendants, and oneself. (1.60)
The Āsura [form] arises from the taking of wealth; the Gāndharva, from mutual agreement;
the Rākṣasa, from abduction by force; and the Paiśāca, from the deception of the maiden. (1.61)

The hand should be taken in marriage from women of the same caste; a Kṣatriya woman should take hold of an arrow, and a Vaiśya woman should take up a goad, while a woman of lower mind should grasp the hem of the garment. 1.62.

The father, the maternal grandfather, a brother, a kinsman, and likewise the mother—each subsequent person among these becomes the giver of the daughter in the absence of the preceding one, provided they are of sound mind. (1.63)
By not giving her away, he incurs the guilt of killing an embryo at every menstrual cycle;
however, in the absence of givers, a maiden may choose a husband for herself from among eligible suitors.
A maiden is given only once; he who carries her off incurs the punishment of a thief.
Even if she has been given away, one may take her back if a more excellent suitor arrives first.
One who gives away a girl without disclosing her defects shall be punished with the highest fine;
he who abandons an unblemished girl, or falsely accuses her of being defiled, shall pay a hundred [paṇas].
Whether she has been violated or not, a remarried woman (punarbhū) is one who has been consecrated again;
likewise, a wanton woman (svairiṇī) is she who, having abandoned her husband, out of desire resorts to a man of her own caste.

If a woman is childless, her brother-in-law or a sapinda or a sagotra, having been anointed with clarified butter and desiring a son, may approach her during her fertile period without the permission of her guru. (1.68)
He may go until the conception of the embryo; otherwise, he would become an outcast.
Born according to this rule, he shall be the son of the owner of the field.
One should cause an unfaithful wife to live deprived of her authority, soiled, subsisting on mere alms, humiliated, and sleeping on the ground. (1.70)
Soma bestowed purity upon women, and the Gandharva gave them graceful speech; Pāvaka granted them the capacity to consume all things, for women are indeed considered sacred. (1.71)
Purification is prescribed after her menstrual period in the case of adultery; however, abandonment is ordained in the event of pregnancy, or if she kills her husband, or commits a great sin. (1.72)
A woman who drinks liquor, one who is diseased, one who is deceitful, one who is barren, one who destroys wealth, one who speaks unpleasantly,
one who bears only daughters, and likewise one who hates her husband— such a wife may be superseded by taking another.
A wife who has been accepted must be supported; otherwise, a great sin would ensue.
Where there is harmony between husband and wife, there the three goals of life flourish. (1.74)
Whether her husband is dead or alive, she who does not approach another man attains fame in this world and rejoices with Umā in the hereafter. (1.75)
The word of the husband must be carried out by the three [classes of wives]; this is the supreme duty of a woman.
Even if he is defiled by a mortal sin (mahāpātaka), he is to be awaited until his purification. 1.76.
Since the attainment of the worlds of infinity and heaven, along with sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, [depends on them], therefore women should be enjoyed, supported, and well-protected. 1.77.
The sixteen nights of women constitute their fertile season; during that time, he should approach his wife on the even nights.
He should remain as one practicing celibacy, avoiding the sacred festival days (parvan) and the first four nights.
Proceeding in this manner, he should avoid a woman who is emaciated, as well as the asterisms Maghā and Mūla;
when the Moon is in a favorable state, a man shall once beget a son endowed with auspicious marks.
Or he may act according to his desire, mindful of the boon granted to women;
yet he should remain devoted to his own wife, for women are declared to be worthy of protection.
Wives should be honored by their husbands, brothers, fathers, kinsmen, mothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, brothers-in-law, and other relatives with ornaments, clothing, and food. (1.81)
With household utensils kept in order, skillful, cheerful, and averse to wasteful expenditure, she, devoted to her husband, should perform the salutation of the feet of her parents-in-law. (1.82)
A woman whose husband is away from home should avoid sporting, grooming her body, attending social gatherings or festivals, laughing, and visiting the houses of others. 1.83.
The father shall protect the maiden; her husband, when she is married; and her son in old age. In the absence of these, her kinsmen shall protect her; a woman never possesses independence. 1.84.
She should not be deprived of her father, mother, son, brother, mother-in-law, father-in-law, or maternal uncles; for without her husband, she would become an object of reproach. (1.85)
If there is another wife of the same caste, he shall not have religious duties performed by her;
among wives of the same caste who are eligible for religious rites, he shall not employ one other than the eldest.
Having cremated his virtuous wife with the *agnihotra* fire, the husband shall,
according to the rule, without delay take another wife and the sacred fires.
Devoted to what is pleasing and beneficial to her husband, well-conducted, and with senses restrained, she attains fame in this world and the unsurpassed state after death. (1.88)
From men of the same caste, born of women of the same caste, indeed arise those of equal birth;
through blameless marriages, sons are born who increase the lineage. (89)
A woman of the Brahmin caste bears a Mūrdhāvasikta from a Kṣatriya; a woman of the Vaiśya caste, an Ambaṣṭha from a Kṣatriya; and a Śūdra woman bears a son called Niṣāda, as well as a Pāraśava.
From a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother, a Māhiṣya and an Ugra are born; from a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya or Śūdra mother, [an Ambaṣṭha and a Niṣāda are born].
From a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother, a Karaṇa is born. This is the rule recorded for those born of wives of different castes.
From a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Sūta; likewise, from a Vaiśya, a Vaidehaka;
and from a Śūdra, a Caṇḍāla is born, who is despised by all righteous laws.
From a Vaiśya father and a Kṣatriya mother, a Māgadha was born; and from a Śūdra father, she likewise gave birth to a Kṣattṛ.
From a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother, the Vaiśya woman indeed begot a son known as an Āyogava. (1.93)
From a Māhiṣya father and a Karaṇī mother, a Rathakāra is born;
these are to be understood as both "untrue" (asat) and "true" (sat), according to their status as inverse (pratiloma) or direct (anuloma) offspring.
An elevation of caste is to be known as occurring in the fifth or even the seventh generation;
upon the reversal of actions, there is equality, and as before, there is the state of being lower or higher. (1.95)

A householder should perform the ritual acts prescribed by the Smṛti every day in the nuptial fire, or in the fire brought at the time of inheritance; however, he should perform the Śrauta rites in the Vaitānika fires.
Having attended to the needs of the body and performed the rites of purification, the twice-born man should perform the morning twilight devotions, preceded by the cleansing of the teeth. 1.97.
Having offered oblations into the fires, he should, with a concentrated mind, recite the mantras dedicated to the Sun-god;
he should master the meanings of the Vedas and various treatises as well. ||1.98||
And he should approach the Lord for the sake of accomplishing his welfare and security;
having bathed, he should likewise gratify and worship the gods and the ancestors. 1.99.

To accomplish the purpose of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña), one should, according to one's ability, recite the Vedas, the Atharva-veda, the Purāṇas along with the Itihāsas, and the spiritual knowledge (adhyātmikī vidyā). 1.100.

The rites for the ancestors (balikarma), the svadhā-oblation, Vedic study, and the hospitable reception of guests are the great sacrifices to the spirits, the ancestors, the gods, Brahmā, and human beings. 1.101.
From the remnants of the food offered to the gods, he should present the *bali* offering to the spirits;
he should also place food on the ground for dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and birds. (1.102)
Food should be given daily to the ancestors and to men, as well as water;
one should perform the private recitation of the Vedas daily, but one should not cook food for oneself alone.
Having first fed the children, the daughters living in the house, the elderly, pregnant women, the sick, young girls, guests, and servants, the husband and wife may eat the remainder. (1.104)
A twice-born man eating his food should likewise perform the *apośāna* rite both before and after; thus the food should be made as if not naked and as if it were nectar. (1.105)
Even when one is a guest, gifts should be given to those of the [social] classes according to one's ability and in due order.
A guest must not be turned away even in the evening, even if only with kind words, a place on the ground, or water. (1.106)
O monks, alms should be given with respect to one who observes the vows; and at the proper time, one should feed friends, relatives, and kinsmen who have arrived. 1.107
One should provide a great bull or a great goat to a learned Brahmin;
[one should also practice] hospitable treatment, service, delicious food, and pleasant speech.

However, every year the following are worthy of the guest-offering (arghya): a Snātaka, a teacher, a king, a dear friend, one for whom one’s daughter is being wedded, and likewise the officiating priests at a sacrifice. (1.109)
A traveler and a learned man who has mastered the Vedas should be known as guests;
these two are to be honored by a householder desiring the world of Brahman. (1.110)
One should not take pleasure in food prepared by others, except when invited by those beyond reproach;
one should avoid fickleness of speech, hands, and feet, as well as overeating. (1.111)
He should follow a guest who is a learned Vedic scholar as far as the boundary of his domain once he is satisfied;
for the remainder of the day, he should sit together with cultured men, beloved friends, and kinsmen. 1.112.
Having performed the evening twilight devotions, having offered oblations into those fires and attended to them,
and having eaten with his dependents without excessive greed, he should then go to rest.
One should not neglect virtue, wealth, and pleasure according to one's capacity;
having risen during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā, one should contemplate what is beneficial for oneself. (1.114)
They are to be honored according to their sequence by virtue of knowledge, ritual action, age, kinship, and wealth;
even a Śūdra, when possessed of an abundance of these, deserves honor in old age. (1.115)

The way must be yielded to the elderly, the burdened, the king, the bath-graduate, women, the sick, ascetics, and those who possess a wheel; among these, O King, the bath-graduate is to be honored even by the monarch.
Sacrificing, studying, and giving are for the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya;
however, for the Brāhmaṇa, there are additionally the receiving of gifts, as well as officiating at sacrifices and teaching. (1.117)
The primary duty of a Kṣatriya is the protection of the subjects; lending money at interest, agriculture, trade, and animal husbandry are prescribed for the Vaiśya. (1.118)

The duty of a Śūdra is service to the twice-born; if he cannot subsist by that, he may become a merchant, or he may live by various crafts, while performing what is beneficial for the twice-born. (1.119)
Delighting in his wife, pure, a supporter of his dependents, and devoted to the performance of ancestral rites,
he shall not neglect the five sacrifices by means of the mantra of salutation.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, restraint of the senses, self-control, forbearance, straightforwardness, and generosity are the means for the practice of dharma for all. 1.121.
One should likewise adopt a conduct that is consistent with one's age, intelligence, wealth, speech, dress, learning, birth, and actions— conduct that is straightforward and free from deceit.
A twice-born man who possesses more than a three-year supply of grain may indeed drink the Soma;
he whose food supply lasts for one year should perform the rites preliminary to the Soma sacrifice.
Every year the Soma sacrifice is to be performed, as well as at each solstice;
likewise, the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices must indeed be performed.
In the absence of these, the twice-born man should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice;
he should not perform a rite with deficient materials when the necessary substances are available, for only then does it yield its fruit.
One who solicits alms from a Śūdra becomes a Caṇḍāla by performing a sacrifice;
one who does not give what was obtained for the sake of a sacrifice is born as a vulture or even a crow. (1.126)

One may possess grain in a granary or a jar, or have enough for three days, or even live from day to day; or one may subsist by gleaning ears of corn or picking up single grains—among these, each succeeding mode is superior to the preceding. (1.127)
One should not strive for wealth that interferes with Vedic study, nor from whatever source it may come;
one should not engage in forbidden pursuits and should always remain contented. 1.128

If one suffers from hunger, one may seek wealth from kings, pupils, or those for whom one performs sacrifices; however, one should not honor those who are hypocritical, those who rely on mere reasoning, heretics, or those who act like herons. 1.129.
Wearing white garments, with his hair, beard, and nails clipped short, and being pure, he shall not eat while looking at his wife, nor while wearing only a single garment, nor while standing. 1.130.
One should not fall into doubt, nor should one speak unpleasantly without cause;
one should neither speak what is harmful nor what is untrue, nor should one be a thief or a usurer. (1.131)
Wearing a sacred thread, carrying a staff and a water-pot,
a follower of Dakṣa should circumambulate clockwise the gods, clay, cows, Brahmins, and trees.
One should not urinate in a river, in the shade, on a path, in a cow-pen, in water, or on ashes;
nor should one do so facing fire, the sun, cows, the moon, the twilight, water, women, or the twice-born. 1.133.
One should not look at the sun, nor at a naked woman, nor at one who has just engaged in sexual intercourse; nor should one look at urine or feces, nor, while impure, at the eclipsed moon or stars.
"This is my vajra"—with these words, he should recite this entire mantra.
He may go about unsheltered even when it rains; he may sleep with his head toward the west, and he must not [fear anything]. (1.135)
One should not throw spittle, blood, feces, urine, or poison into water;
one should not warm one's feet over a fire, nor should one step over it. (1.136)
One should not drink water from one's cupped hands, nor should one awaken a sleeping person.
One should not play with dice, nor should one dwell with those who destroy dharma or with those afflicted by disease. (1.137)
One should avoid prohibited actions, the smoke from a funeral pyre, crossing a river [by swimming], and staying upon hair, ashes, chaff, embers, or skull-bones. (1.138)
One should not point out a cow suckling her calf, nor should one ever enter through any place other than the gate;
one should not accept gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures.
In receiving gifts, the butcher, the oil-presser, the gambler, the prostitute, and the king are wicked;
each of these is ten times more wicked than the one preceding it. (1.140)

The commencement of the study of the chapters (of the Vedas) takes place on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa when the moon is in conjunction with the asterism Śravaṇa, or under the asterism Hasta, or when the medicinal herbs appear, or on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
On the day of Rohiṇī in the month of Pauṣa, or likewise on the Aṣṭakā day,
a twice-born man should perform the formal conclusion of the Vedic studies (utsarga) at the water's edge according to the prescribed rule.
There is a suspension of study for three days in the event of a death among pupils, officiating priests, teachers, or kinsmen;
likewise upon the commencement (upākarma) and conclusion (utsarga) of the Vedic term, and when a Śrotriya of one's own Vedic school has died. 1.143.
In the event of thunder at twilight, a lightning strike, an earthquake, or the fall of a meteor, one should remain impure for a day and night;
likewise after completing the study of the Veda or having studied the Āraṇyaka.
On the fifteenth day, the fourteenth day, or the eighth day; during an eclipse of Rāhu; at the transitions of the seasons; or having eaten, or having accepted a gift at a Śrāddha ceremony. ||1.145||

When an animal, a frog, a mongoose, a dog, a snake, a cat, or a pig has passed through [the space between the thumb and forefinger], it constitutes a day and night; likewise when there is a fall or a rising of Śakra.
In the presence of the sound of dogs, jackals, donkeys, owls, the *sāman* chants, or the cries of those afflicted by arrows;
or near impure substances, a corpse, a *śūdra*, an outcaste, a cemetery, or one who has fallen from his caste. (1.147)
In an impure place, or when one is oneself impure; during a flash of lightning or a clap of thunder;
after eating while the hands are still wet; while in water; at midnight; or during an excessive windstorm—[one should not study]. (1.148)

When there is a rain of dust, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, during the fears of twilight or mist, when there is a foul odor, and when a learned man has come to one's house—one should run [to greet him]. (1.149)

When there is the sound of donkeys, camels, vehicles, elephants, horses, or boats, or when trees fall and mountains crumble—these thirty-seven occasions are known as temporary interruptions for study. 1.150.
One should not step on the shadow of a deity, a sacrificial priest, a snātaka, a teacher, or a king, nor that of another person;
nor should one step on blood, feces, urine, spittle, or the remains of an ointment.
Brahmins and Kshatriyas should never be treated with contempt;
until death one should desire prosperity, and one should not strike anyone at their vital points.
One should discard remnants of food, excrement, urine, and water from the feet at a distance;
one should always properly practice the conduct prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti. (1.153)
One who is impure from eating should not touch cows, Brahmins, fire, or food, nor should he touch them with his foot.
He should not engage in reviling or beating them; however, he may strike his son or his pupil.
One should practice dharma with effort through deed, mind, and speech; however, one should not practice even that which is dharma if it is contrary to the scriptures or despised by the world. 1.155
With mother, father, guests, brothers, kinsmen, relatives, maternal uncles, the elderly, children, the sick, teachers, physicians, dependents, and friends; || 1.156 ||
Having avoided disputes with officiating priests, family chaplains, ministers, wives, slaves, and kinsmen, the householder shall conquer all worlds. (1.157)
One should not bathe in the waters of others without first removing five lumps [of earth];
one may, however, bathe in rivers, natural ponds, lakes, and reservoirs.

One should avoid the bed, seat, garden, house, and vehicle of another if they have not been given; nor should one eat the food of one who maintains no sacred fire, except in times of distress. (1.159)
[The food] of misers, bound thieves, eunuchs, actors,
bamboo-workers, those accused of crimes, usurers, courtesans, and those initiated into a multitude [of heretics]— ||1.160||
[One should not study] in the presence of a physician, a sick person, one who is angry, an unchaste woman, one who is intoxicated, or an enemy;
nor in the presence of one who is cruel, fierce, fallen, an outcaste, a hypocrite, or one who eats the remnants of others' food. (1.161)

[The impurity lasts for one day] for those whose wives have no husbands, for goldsmiths, for those who have been conquered by their wives, for village-priests, for sellers of weapons, for blacksmiths, for weavers, and for those who live by keeping dogs. (11.62)

[One should not accept gifts] from a cruel man, a king, a dyer, an ungrateful person, one who lives by slaughter, a laundryman, a cultivator of the earth, one who lives with a paramour, or a householder [who harbors such persons]. (1.163)
One must not eat the food of these, nor that of a seller of Soma, nor of a slanderer or a liar, nor likewise of a wheelwright or a professional bard. (1.164)

Food that has not been honored, meat not intended for sacrifice, food containing hair or insects, that which has turned sour, stale food, leavings, food touched by a dog, or food looked upon by an outcast; 1.165.

One should avoid food touched by a woman in her courses, food that has been publicly proclaimed [as such], and food over which someone has sipped water; likewise, food smelled by a cow, food left over from birds, and food intentionally touched by the feet. (1.166)
Among Śūdras, the food of a slave, a cowherd, a family friend, and a sharecropper may be eaten; likewise that of a barber and one who offers himself as a servant. 1.167.
Food that has stood overnight may be eaten if it is mixed with oil or fat, even if it has been kept for a long time;
likewise, preparations of wheat, barley, and cow's milk products may be eaten even if they are not oily.

One should avoid the milk of a cow that is in heat, one whose calf has not yet passed ten days, or one that is nursing; likewise, the milk of camels, of animals with uncloven hoofs, of women, of wild animals, and of sheep. (1.169)

One should avoid sacrificial offerings intended for deities, the śigru plant, blood, the wood used for cutting, meat that has not been consecrated by ritual slaughter, substances produced from excrement, and mushrooms. (1.170)
Flesh-eating birds, the dātyūha, the parrot, pecking birds, the ṭiṭṭibha, the sārasa crane, single-hoofed animals, swans, and all village-dwelling birds. 1.171.
The koyaṣṭi, plava, cakravāka, balākā, and baka birds, as well as grain-scattering birds;
and *kṛsara*, *saṃyāva*, *pāyasa*, cakes, and fried pastries—these, when consumed for no sacred purpose, [are forbidden]. 1.172.
The *kalaviṅka*, the *kākola*, the *kurara*, the *rajjudālaka*, web-footed birds, the *khañjarīṭa*, and wild animals or birds that are unknown [should not be eaten]. (1.173)
Having unintentionally eaten blue jays, red-footed birds, dog meat, dried meat, or fish, one shall fast for three days. (1.174)
Having eaten onions, a village pig, a mushroom, a village cock, garlic, or leeks, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (1.175)
Among five-toed animals, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, the tortoise, the hedgehog, and the hare may be eaten; and among fish, the siṃhatuṇḍaka and the rohita may likewise be consumed. (1.176)
Likewise, the pāṭhīna, the rājīva, and fish with scales may be eaten by the twice-born;
therefore, hear now the rules regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat. (1.177)

In a life-threatening emergency, at a Śrāddha ceremony, when consecrated by sprinkling, or at the desire of a Brāhmaṇa—eating meat after having worshipped the gods and the ancestors, one incurs no fault. (1.178)
That man of evil conduct who kills animals contrary to the prescribed rule shall dwell in a terrible hell for as many days as there are hairs on the bodies of those animals. (1.179)
By abstaining from meat, a brahmin who lives as a sage even while residing at home attains all his desires as well as the fruit of the horse sacrifice. (1.180)
Of golden and silver lotuses, of vessels for holding [liquids], of stones, of vegetables, ropes, roots, fruits, garments, split bamboo, and skins; ||1.181||
The purification of bowls and cups is prescribed by means of water;
however, vessels for the *caru* oblation, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and vessels containing oily substances are purified with hot water. (1.182)

The sprinkling of the wooden sword, the winnowing basket, the skin, the grain, the pestle, the mortar, and the fire-drills, as well as of many objects joined together and of numerous garments, is prescribed. (1.183)
Wooden, horn, and bone vessels are to be scraped; those made of fruit are to be scrubbed with cow-hair;
and sacrificial vessels during a ritual act are to be wiped with the hand. 1.184.
Woolen cloth and spun-silk are purified with water and cow's urine containing soap-berries; similarly, fine silk and deerskin are purified with water and myrobalan.
Linen cloth purified by white mustard seeds, earthenware by re-firing, the hand of an artisan, merchandise, alms-food, and likewise the mouth of a woman—these are pure. (1.186)

The purification of the ground is achieved through sweeping, burning, the passage of time, the treading of cows, as well as sprinkling, scraping, and smearing; likewise, a house is purified by sweeping and smearing. (1.187)
When food has been smelled by a cow, or is defiled by hair, flies, or insects, water, ashes, or even earth should be sprinkled upon it for the sake of purification. (1.188)
The purification of tin, lead, and copper is by means of alkaline substances, acids, water, and liquids; that of bell-metal and iron is by ashes; but for a liquid, it is by straining.
The purification of that which is smeared with impurity is by means of earth and water until the odor is removed;
what is commended by word, what is washed with water, and what is unknown are always pure. (1.190)
Water on the ground that is naturally pure and sufficient for one's thirst is clean;
likewise is meat fallen from a dog, a caṇḍāla, a carnivorous beast, or the like. (1.191)
A ray of light, fire, dust, a shadow, a cow, a horse, the earth, and the wind;
droplets of water, flies, and a calf during the act of suckling—these are pure when touched. (1.192)
The goat and the horse are pure in their mouths; neither the cow nor those born from humans are impure;
and roads are purified by the rays of the moon and sun and by the wind. (1.193)

Drops from the mouth are pure, as are drops from the final rinsing; likewise, the beard that enters the mouth and what is stuck between the teeth do not defile one, provided they are removed, after which one becomes pure. (1.194)
The mud and water in a street that have been touched by outcastes, dogs,
or crows are purified by the wind alone, as are structures built of baked bricks.
Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, walked upon a road, or changed one's garment, one who has already sipped water (ācamana) should sip water again. 1.196.
Having performed austerities, Brahmā created the Brāhmaṇas for the protection of the Vedas, for the satisfaction of the ancestors and the gods, and for the preservation of Dharma. (1.197)
The Brahmins who are devoted to sacred learning and study are the source of all;
those devoted to ritual action are superior to them, but those who contemplate the supreme self are indeed superior to them. (1.198)

Neither by knowledge alone nor even by austerity is one a worthy recipient; that in which both conduct and these two [knowledge and austerity] reside is indeed proclaimed to be a worthy recipient. 1.199.
Cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth should be given with honor to a worthy recipient;
nothing at all should be given to an unworthy recipient by a wise person who desires his own welfare. (1.200)
One who is devoid of both knowledge and austerity should not accept a gift;
by accepting one, he leads both the giver and himself downward. (1.201)
One should give daily to a worthy recipient, especially on auspicious occasions;
even when asked, one should give according to one's ability, purified by faith. (1.202)
A milch cow of good disposition, with horns tipped in gold and hooves in silver, accompanied by a cloth, a bronze milking vessel, and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), should be given away.
The giver of this [cow] attains heaven for as many years as there are hairs on her body;
if she is tawny (kapilā), she further delivers his lineage up to the seventh generation.
By giving a cow with its calf and facing both ways according to the previously mentioned rite, the donor attains heaven for as many ages as there are hairs on its body.
By giving a cow, whether it be a milch cow or even one that is not, provided it is healthy and free from affliction, the donor shall attain heaven. (1.206)

Massaging those who are weary, attending to the sick, worshiping the gods, washing the feet of others, and clearing away the remnants of food from twice-born men are equal to the gift of a cow. (1.207)
By giving land, cattle, food, clothing, water, sesame seeds, clarified butter, shelter,
a dwelling, gold, or a draft animal, one is glorified in heaven.
By giving a house, grain, fearlessness, sandals, an umbrella, garlands, ointments, a vehicle, water, or a bed, one becomes supremely happy. (1.209)
Brahman consists of all dharmas; therefore, it is superior to all gifts. By bestowing that, one attains the world of Brahmā, never falling away from it. ||1.210||
Even though he is capable of accepting gifts, he who does not accept them attains those abundant worlds which belong to those whose nature is generosity. ||1.211||
Kuśa grass, vegetables, milk, fish, perfumes, flowers, curd, earth, meat, bedding, a seat, and grain—these may be refused, but not water. (1.212)
One may accept food brought unasked even from a person of evil deeds, except in the case of an unchaste woman, a eunuch, an outcast, or an enemy. (1.213)
One may accept gifts from anyone for the sake of honoring guests, for the purpose of maintaining one's teacher, and indeed for the sake of one's own subsistence. (1.214)

The new moon day, the eight-day festivals, the occasion of prosperity, the dark fortnight, the two solstices, the excellence of materials and Brahmins, the equinoxes, and the sun's passage into a zodiacal sign. (1.215)
Vyatīpāta, Gajacchāyā, the eclipses of the moon and the sun,
and a personal inclination toward performing a Śrāddha— these are proclaimed as the times for Śrāddha.

He is the foremost among all those learned in the Vedas, a śrotriya, a knower of the Veda, and young; he understands the meaning of the Veda, is a master of the Jyeṣṭhasāman, and has mastered the Trimadhu and Trisuparṇa hymns. ||1.217||

A sister's son, an officiating priest, a son-in-law, a person for whom one sacrifices, a father-in-law, a maternal uncle, one who has mastered the Triṇāciketa fire-sacrifice, a daughter's son, a pupil, a relative by marriage, and a kinsman; ||1.218||

Brahmins who are devoted to ritual action, devoted to austerity, who maintain the five fires, who are celibate students, and who are dedicated to their fathers and mothers, bring prosperity to the śrāddha.

One who is diseased, deficient or redundant in limb, one-eyed, born of a remarried woman, one who has broken his vow of chastity, the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, one with deformed nails, and one with black teeth; 1.220.

One who teaches for wages, one who is cruel, one who defiles a maiden, one who is falsely accused, one who betrays a friend, a slanderer, a seller of Soma, and one who marries before his elder brother; 1.221.

One who abandons his mother, father, or son; one who eats food from a *kuṇḍa* (an illegitimate vessel); the son of a *vṛṣala*; the husband of a woman previously married to another; a thief; and one whose actions are corrupt—these are the censured. 1.222.
On the day before [the ceremony], the self-possessed and pure host should invite the Brahmins;
and those invited must remain restrained in mind, speech, and body. (1.223)
Having honored those who have arrived with a welcome in the afternoon,
the priest, with purificatory grass in hand, should seat them on their seats after they have sipped water for purification.

At a rite for the gods, he should feed an even number of guests according to his ability, and likewise an odd number at a rite for the ancestors; this should be done in a secluded, clean place that slopes toward the south.
Two for the gods, facing east; three for the ancestors, facing north; or one for each.
The same applies to the maternal grandfathers, or the Vaiśvadeva rite may be performed as a single common offering.
Having given water for washing the hands and also *kuśa* grass for the seats, he should, being authorized, invoke [the ancestors] with the *ṛc* verse beginning "O Viśvedevas... (RV 7.38.1).
Then, having scattered barley over a vessel containing a strainer, and having poured water with the verse "śaṃ no devīr," he should throw barley grains with the formula "yavo 'si. (1.228)
With the mantra "yā divyā," one should pour the *arghya* water into their hands;
having offered water, one should present perfumes, incense, garlands, and lamps. (1.229)

Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (aprasavya) and circumambulating the ancestors counter-clockwise, he should offer double-folded kuśa grass while reciting the verse beginning with "uṣantas tvā. (1.230)
Having invoked [the deities], one should recite the mantra "May they come to us" (Āyantu naḥ) with their permission;
one should use sesame seeds instead of barley, while the remaining rites, such as the *arghya* offering and so forth, are to be performed as before.
Having offered the *arghya* water and having placed their remnants in a vessel according to the rule,
he turns the vessel face down with the words "This is the seat for the ancestors," placing it below.
Intending to offer it in the fire, he takes up food soaked in clarified butter and asks, "Do so.
Having been permitted with the words, "Do so," he offers it into the fire according to the ritual for the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña).
With a concentrated mind, he should offer the remnants of the oblation into vessels,
especially those made of silver, as they may be obtained.
Having given the food, one should consecrate the vessel with the mantra, "The earth is the vessel";
then, having recited "Idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," one should cause the big toes of the twice-born to touch the food.
Having recited the Sāvitrī together with the Vyahṛtis, and the three verses beginning with "madhu vātā," they should eat while remaining silent, speaking only as much as necessary for comfort.
Free from anger and without haste, he should offer the desired food and sacrificial oblations;
likewise, having recited the purificatory mantras and the previously mentioned prayers until satiety, he should proceed.
Having taken food, and having ascertained that they are satisfied and have permitted the remainder,
one should scatter that food upon the ground and offer water once, then once again.
Taking all the food together with sesame seeds, facing the south,
he should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) near the remains of the meal, as in the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña).
In the same manner, one should likewise offer water for sipping to the maternal grandfathers;
then, having caused the benediction (svasti) to be recited, one should offer the water for imperishability (akṣayyodaka).
Having given the sacrificial fee according to his ability, he should utter the word *svadhā*.
Being authorized with the words "Let it be spoken," he should say, "Let *svadhā* be uttered for the ancestors. (1.241)
When they have said, "Let there be *svadhā*," he should then pour water upon the ground;
saying, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," he thus offers the water. (1.242)
"May our donors increase, as may the lineage of the Vedas;
may our faith not depart, and may we have much to give. (1.243)
Having repeatedly spoken pleasant words and having prostrated, one should dismiss [the guests] with joy, saying "Vāja! Vāja! while performing the dismissal starting with the ancestors.
Having turned face upwards that vessel for the ancestors into which those remnants were previously poured into the *arghya* bowl, he should dismiss the Brahmins. (1.245)
Having circumambulated [the vessel] from left to right, he should eat what was served to the ancestors;
remaining celibate and self-restrained, he should spend that night together with the twice-born.
Having thus performed the circumambulation, they worship the Nāndīmukha ancestors during the rite for prosperity;
the offerings consist of balls of rice mixed with curd and jujube fruit, and the rituals are performed with barley.
The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is devoid of the deities, possesses only one *arghya* offering and one *pavitraka*,
is free from the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and pouring into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*).
At the point where the word "akṣayya" (imperishable) occurs, one should say "upatiṣṭhatām" (may it attend) during the dismissal of the Brahmins;
one should say "abhiramyatām" (may you be pleased), and they should reply, "We have been pleased. (1.249)
One should prepare four vessels containing scented water and sesame seeds;
for the purpose of the *arghya* offering, one should pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors (*pitṛ*).
With the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ," the remainder—starting with the offering of water (arghya) and so forth—is as before.
This Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite is also performed for a woman in the same manner as the Ekoddiṣṭa.
For one whose sapindikarana has taken place before the completion of a year,
one should give food along with a water-pot to a twice-born man for the duration of that year.
On the anniversary of the day of death, the Śrāddha should be performed every month for a year,
and likewise once a year thereafter, in accordance with the purpose of the monthly rites.
One should give the morsels of food to cows, goats, or Brahmins, or else throw them into fire or water;
while virtuous Brahmins are present, one must not clear away the remnants of the twice-born's meal.
Indeed, by means of sacrificial food (haviṣya) one [attains the fruit] for a month, but by milk-rice (pāyasa) for a year;
likewise by fish, deer, mutton, poultry, goat, and the meat of the spotted deer.
The ancestors here are indeed satisfied by the offerings of the meat of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, the boar, and the hare, respectively, as the months increase. (1.256)
The flesh of rhinoceroses, large-scaled fish, honey, and the food of sages;
the flesh of iron-eating creatures, black pot-herbs, and the meat of the vārdhrāṇasa crane.
Whatever one gives while staying at Gayā, all that becomes infinite;
likewise on the thirteenth day of the month and under the Maghā asterism, there is no doubt. ||1.258||
Daughters and those who seek daughters, principal cattle, even sons, gambling, agriculture and trade, as well as animals with cloven and uncloven hoofs; 1.259.
The giver of the Śrāddha always obtains sons endowed with Vedic luster, gold, silver, and base metals, preeminence among kinsmen, and all desires. (1.260)
Indeed, excluding those killed by weapons from the first day of the lunar fortnight up to the fourteenth, offerings are presented there for them.
For [he grants] heaven, offspring, vigor, heroism, a field, and likewise strength; sons, preeminence, good fortune, progeny, and the status of being the chief among sons.
The turning of the wheel [of Dharma], sons, sovereignty over kinsmen, as well as freedom from disease, fame, freedom from sorrow, and the supreme goal—these he bestowed. (1.263)
He who offers a śrāddha according to the rule bestows wealth, knowledge, success in medicine, base metals, cattle, goats and sheep, horses, and long life. (1.264)
From Kṛttikā to Bharaṇī, he who is a believer, full of faith, and free from pride and envy, shall obtain these desires. (1.265)
The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the ancestors who are the deities of the śrāddha;
when satiated by the śrāddha, they gratify the ancestors of human beings.
When pleased, the ancestors bestow upon men longevity, wisdom, wealth, learning, heaven, liberation, and pleasures, as well as sovereignty. (1.267)
In ancient times, Vināyaka was appointed by Rudra and Brahmā for the sake of presiding over the Gaṇas and for the successful accomplishment of actions hindered by obstacles. (1.268)
Learn now the symptoms of one who is afflicted by that:
in a dream, he plunges excessively into water and sees shaven-headed men. (1.269)
He wears saffron-colored garments and mounts carnivorous beasts;
he dwells together with outcastes, donkeys, and camels. (1.270)
Likewise, while walking, he imagines himself followed by others;
dejected and with his undertakings frustrated, he sinks down without apparent cause. (1.271)
Afflicted by that, the prince does not obtain a kingdom;
nor does the maiden obtain a husband, nor offspring, nor even a fetus. (1.272)
Being a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), one does not obtain the status of a teacher; likewise, a student does not obtain his studies.
A merchant does not obtain profit, nor does a farmer obtain the fruits of his cultivation. (1.273)
On an auspicious day, his ceremonial bath (snapana) should be performed according to the prescribed ritual;
he should first be smeared with a paste of white mustard seeds mixed with curd.
Likewise, with his head anointed with all medicinal herbs and all fragrant substances,
and seated upon an auspicious throne, he should have virtuous brahmins recite benedictions.

One should throw into the water earth from a stable for horses, from a stable for elephants, from an anthill, from a confluence, and from a pool, as well as yellow pigment, fragrant substances, and guggulu resin.
The water brought from the lake in four jars of a single color,
as well as the auspicious seat (bhadrāsana), should be placed upon a red bull's hide.
With that which has a thousand eyes and a hundred streams, purified by the seers—I sprinkle you with it; may the purifying verses cleanse you. (278)
King Varuṇa gave you fortune; Sūrya and Bṛhaspati gave you fortune;
Indra and Vāyu gave you fortune; and the Seven Seers gave you fortune. (1.279)
Whatever misfortune is in your hair, in the parting of your hair, or on your head; whatever is on your forehead, in your ears, or in your eyes—may the waters always destroy that for you. 1.280
Having bathed, one should offer mustard oil with a ladle made of udumbara wood into the head, while grasping the kuśa grass with the left hand.
One should recite the names of Mita, Saṃmita, Sālakaṭaṅkaṭa, and Kūśmāṇḍarājaputra, accompanied by the word "svāhā."
Having spread *kuśa* grass in every direction upon a winnowing basket at a crossroads, one should offer [the oblation] with their names and with *bali*-mantras accompanied by salutations. (1.283)
Rice grains both prepared and unprepared, as well as rice mixed with minced meat;
likewise, fish both cooked and raw, and meat—just these [were offered]. (1.284)
Variegated and fragrant flowers, the three kinds of liquor, radishes, *pūrikā* cakes, *apūpa* cakes, as well as *uḍḍeraka* pastries and garlands; 1.285.
Having offered the *arghya* consisting of a full *añjali* of a paste made from *dūrvā* grass and mustard seeds,
he should then worship Ambikā, the mother of Vināyaka.
Grant me beauty, grant me fame, and grant me fortune; grant me sons, grant me auspicious prosperity, and grant me all my desires.
Wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands, perfumes, and ointments,
he should feed the Brahmins and also give a pair of garments to his preceptor.
Having thus worshipped Vināyaka and the planets according to the prescribed rule,
one obtains the fruit of one's actions and attains unsurpassed prosperity.
By constantly performing worship of Āditya, as well as Tilakasvāmin and Mahāgaṇapati, one shall attain success.
One who desires prosperity, or one who desires peace, or one who desires rain, long life, and nourishment, or likewise one performing malevolent rites, should undertake the sacrifice to the planets.
The Sun, the Moon, the Son of the Earth (Mars), the Son of the Moon (Mercury), Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and Ketu—these are remembered as the planets. ||1.292||
These planets should be fashioned in order from copper, crystal, red sandalwood, gold, silver, iron, and lead. (1.293)
They should be drawn on a cloth with their own respective colors, or upon fragrant mandalas;
garments and flowers should be offered according to their respective colors. (1.294)
Fragrances and offerings, as well as incense with guggulu resin, should be presented; and sacrificial oblations (caru) accompanied by ritual threads must be prepared for each respective deity.
The verses "ākṛṣṇena," "imaṃ devāḥ," "agnir mūrdhā divaḥ kakut," and "udbudhyasva" are proclaimed in their respective order. ||1.296||
"Bṛhaspate atyāryaḥ," "tathaivānnāt parisrutaḥ," "śaṃ no devīḥ," and likewise "kāṇḍāt ketuṃ kṛṇvan"—these [verses] as well. 1.297.
Arka, palāśa, khadira, apāmārga, then pippala, udumbara, śamī, dūrvā, and kuśa are the sacrificial fuels (samidh) in their respective order. ||1.298||
For each of these, one hundred and eight or twenty-eight oblations should be offered, mixed with honey, clarified butter, and curd.
Rice with molasses, milk-rice, sacrificial food, rice mixed with milk and ṣaṣṭika grain, curd-rice, clarified butter, cakes, meat, and variegated foods. 1.300

A wise man should give this food to the twice-born according to the sequence of the planets, honoring them with due ceremony and according to his ability or as it may be obtained, in accordance with the prescribed rite. 1.301.
One should give as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) in sequence: a cow, a conch shell, a bull, gold, a garment, a horse, a black cow, iron, and a goat. 1.302.
Whoever is in distress at any time should honor him with effort;
for this boon was granted to them by Brahmā: "When you are honored, you shall in turn honor [others]. (1.303)
The rise and fall of kings, as well as the existence and non-existence of the world, are dependent upon the planets; therefore, the planets are most worthy of worship. (1.304)
He was possessed of great energy, liberal, grateful, a servant of the elders, humble, endowed with courage, of noble birth, truthful in speech, and pure. ||1.305||
He is not dilatory, possesses mindfulness, and likewise has a retinue that is not mean-spirited;
he is righteous, firm in devotion, wise, heroic, and a knower of secrets. (1.306)

That lord of men was likewise trained in the protection of his own vulnerabilities through the science of logic and the science of government, as well as in the science of economics and the triple Vedas.
He should appoint ministers who are wise, hereditary, steadfast, and pure;
with them he should deliberate on state affairs, and thereafter with a Brahmin, and finally by himself.

And he should appoint as his domestic priest one who is renowned for his learning, skilled in astrology, and likewise proficient in the science of government as well as the Atharvāṅgiras [Veda]. (1.309)

For the sake of performing rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, he should likewise choose officiating priests and conduct sacrifices according to the rules, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
One should give enjoyments and various riches to the Brahmins;
for that which is bestowed upon Brahmins is an inexhaustible treasure for kings. (1.311)

That which is not spilled, which is without injury, and which is not defiled by expiatory rites—such an offering made from one fire into the fire of a Brahmin is said here to be the most excellent. (1.312)

One should strive to obtain what has not been obtained; one should protect with effort what has been obtained; one should constantly increase what has been protected; and one should bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients. ||1.313||
Having granted land or established a fixed endowment, the king should cause a written deed to be made for the information of future minor rulers. (1.314)
On a cloth or on a copper plate,
the lord of the earth, having inscribed his own lineage and himself, should mark it with his own seal.
One should cause a stable edict to be issued, specifying the dimensions of the land received, describing the boundaries of the gift, and provided with one's own signature and the date. 1.316.

He should take refuge in a region that is pleasant, favorable to cattle, providing a good livelihood, and of the *jāṅgala* type; there he should construct fortresses for the increase of his people, treasury, and self. (1.317)
In each of those matters, he should appoint supervisors who are expert, skillful, pure, and diligent in the affairs of revenue and expenditure. (1.318)
There is no duty for kings higher than this: that wealth acquired in battle is given to the Brahmins, and constant fearlessness is granted to the subjects. (1.319)
Those who are slain in battles for the sake of land, without turning their backs and with weapons free from deceit, go to heaven just like yogins.
When those who do not retreat have been broken, the king takes away their merits, as well as the merits of those who were slain while fleeing. (1.321)

One should not strike one who proclaims "I am yours," nor a eunuch, nor one who is unarmed, nor one who has joined another's side, nor one who has turned away, nor even a spectator of the battle. 1.322.
Having performed the protective rites, he should rise and personally inspect income and expenditure; then, having attended to legal affairs, he should bathe and eat according to his desire. (1.323)
Then, he should deposit the gold brought by the officials into the treasury;
thereafter, having consulted with his ministers, he should inspect his spies and dispatch his envoys.
Then he may move about at his own pleasure, or associate with his ministers;
having inspected the forces, he should deliberate together with the commander-in-chief.
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should listen to the secret speech of his spies;
he should enjoy himself with songs and dances, and likewise recite his private Vedic study.
One should go to sleep to the sound of musical instruments and likewise awaken; having awakened, one should reflect upon the scriptures as well as all that is to be done.
Then, having been greeted with blessings by the officiating priests, the family chaplain, and the teachers, he should respectfully dispatch spies among his own people and those of others. (1.328)
Having seen the astrologers and physicians, he gave them cows, gold, and land,
as well as dwellings and houses for those learned in the Vedas.

A king should be patient toward brahmins, straightforward toward his affectionate subjects, and wrathful toward his enemies; he should behave toward his circle of servants and his subjects as a father does.
By protecting [his subjects] according to justice, he takes a sixth part of their merit;
for protection according to justice is superior to all forms of giving. (1.331)
The subjects must be protected from flatterers, thieves, evildoers, violent criminals, and the like, and especially from the scribes. (1.332)
Whatever sin the subjects commit when they are not protected,
half of that belongs to the king, since he receives taxes from them.
Having learned through spies the conduct of those appointed over the kingdom,
he should always honor the virtuous, but put to death those who are the opposite.
Having deprived those who live by bribery of their wealth, he should banish them;
he should always cause those learned in the Vedas (śrotriyas) to dwell [in his realm] with gifts, honor, and hospitality. (1.335)
That king who increases his own treasury from the kingdom by unjust means shall, before long, lose his royal fortune and meet with destruction along with his kinsmen. (1.336)
The fire born from the torment of oppressing the subjects does not turn back until it has consumed the king's lineage, his fortune, and his very life. (1.337)
Whatever dharma exists for a king in the protection of his own kingdom, that very same dharma he obtains in its entirety when bringing another's kingdom under his control. (1.338)
Whatever conduct, whatever legal practice, and whatever established custom exists in a particular family, that very same must be maintained when [the conqueror] has come under their control. (1.339)
Since the kingdom has its root in counsel, he should keep his counsel well-guarded, so that others do not know it until the results of his actions have come to fruition. (1.340)

The enemy, the friend, the neutral, the immediate neighbor, the one beyond him, and the one beyond that—this circle of states should be considered in due order, employing the strategic means beginning with conciliation (sāman). 1.341.
The means—conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and likewise force—will succeed when properly employed; yet force is the resort of those who have no other way. (1.342)
One should properly deliberate upon these qualities: peace, war, marching, halting, seeking refuge, and duplicity. (31.43)
When the enemy kingdom is endowed with excellent qualities, then one should march; provided that the enemy is weak while one's own self possesses joyful mounts and men. (1.344)
Success is established upon two factors: destiny and human effort;
therein, destiny is that which was manifested through human effort in a previous life. (1.345)
Some goals of men are accomplished through destiny, some through chance, and some through human effort; yet among these, human effort is their primary source. (1.346)
For just as a chariot cannot move with only a single wheel, so too destiny does not succeed without human effort. (1.347)
Since the acquisition of a friend is superior to the acquisition of gold or land, one should strive to attain that; thus, being composed, one should protect the truth. (1.348)
The sovereign, the minister, the people, the fortress, the treasury, the army, and likewise the allies—these are the constituent elements; the kingdom is said to have seven limbs. (1.349)
Having obtained that [kingdom], the king should inflict punishment upon the wicked;
for Dharma was created by Brahmā in the form of punishment in ancient times.
He cannot be led astray from this by one who is greedy and of undisciplined mind;
rather, he is led by one who is true to his word, pure, possessed of good companions, and wise. (1.351)
When employed according to the scriptures, it shall bring joy to the entire world—including its gods, asuras, and humans; otherwise, however, it would provoke their wrath. (1.252)
Unjust punishment destroys the world, heaven, and fame;
but just punishment brings a king heaven, fame, and victory. (1.353)
Whether it be a brother, a son worthy of honor, a father-in-law, or even a maternal uncle—there is no one who, having deviated from his own duty, is exempt from punishment by the king. (1.354)
The king who punishes those deserving of punishment and causes those deserving of death to be executed properly, has performed sacrifices with hundreds and thousands of sacrificial fees. (1.355)
Having reflected thus, the king, surrounded by his councilors, should personally examine the legal cases daily, each one separately, for they yield fruit equal to that of a sacrifice. (1.356)
The mote of dust seen in a sunbeam passing through a lattice is known as a *trasareṇu*;
eight of those make one *likṣā*, and three of those are called a *rājasarṣapa*. (1.357)
Three *gaura* make one *yava*; three of those middle-sized *yavas* make one *kṛṣṇala*; five of those *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*; and sixteen of those *māṣas* make one *suvarṇa*.
Four or five *suvarṇas* are proclaimed to be one *pala*;
a silver *māṣa* consists of two *kṛṣṇalas*, and sixteen of those make one *dharaṇa*. (1.359)
Ten *dharaṇas* make one *śatamāna*, which is also a *pala*;
four *suvarṇas* make one *niṣka*; and a copper coin weighing one *kārṣika* is a *paṇa*.
A fine of eighty thousand paṇas is called the highest amercement;
half of that is declared the middle, and half of that is recorded as the lowest.

The punishment of speech, the punishment of reproach, the punishment of fines, and likewise corporal punishment—these should be applied either individually or collectively, according to the gravity of the offense. (1.362)
Having ascertained the offense, as well as the place, the time, and the strength [of the offender],
and having also considered age, action, and wealth, one should determine the punishment.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Conduct," in the Dharmaśāstra of Yājñavalkya.
The Chapter on Legal Procedure (Vyavahārādhyāya)
Free from anger and greed, the king should examine legal cases together with learned Brāhmaṇas, in accordance with the treatises on Dharma. (2.1)
The king should appoint as members of his assembly those who are accomplished in learning and study, of noble birth, speakers of truth, and impartial toward both enemy and friend. (2.2)

If, however, due to the demands of business, the king is unable to oversee legal proceedings himself, he must appoint a Brāhmaṇa who knows all the laws to preside over them together with the court members. 2.3.

If members of the court act with loss of mindfulness or otherwise, whether out of passion, hatred, or even fear, they shall each be punished individually with a fine of twice the amount in dispute. (2.4)
When one who has not been overcome by others through a path devoid of mindfulness and right conduct brings a matter before the king, that indeed constitutes a legal case.
The defendant shall write down in his presence that which has been stated by the plaintiff, marked with the year, month, fortnight, day, name, caste, and other identifying characteristics. (2.6)
The reply to the matter heard [by the court] shall be written in the presence of the plaintiff; thereafter, the defendant shall immediately set forth the proof for the matter he has asserted. (2.7)
Upon the establishment of that, one attains success; otherwise, the opposite occurs.
This four-footed procedure has been demonstrated for use in legal disputes. (2.8)
One should not bring a counter-charge against someone without having first fully discharged one's own accusation;
nor should one cause a person already accused by another to undergo a change of state without evidence. (2.9)
But in cases of assault and violent crimes, one may bring a counter-charge;
in both instances, a surety capable of standing for the determination of the case must be accepted. (2.10)
If he denies it, he should pay the debt to the creditor and an equal amount to the king;
one who brings a false accusation shall pay double the amount of the claim to the king. (2.11)

In cases involving violence, theft, verbal abuse, or the false accusation of a cow or a relative, as well as in disputes concerning women, one should initiate the lawsuit immediately; in other matters, the time may be according to the parties' wish. 2.12.
He goes from one place to another, laps his lips, his forehead perspires, and his face turns pale. (2.13)
With speech parched and faltering, he speaks much that is contradictory;
he does not honor his words or his eyes, and likewise distorts his lips. (2.14)
If one undergoes a change from their natural state through actions of mind, speech, or body during a legal proceeding or when giving testimony, they are proclaimed to be a corrupt person. ||2.15||
He who attempts to prove a doubtful matter on his own authority, he who absconds, or he who says nothing when summoned, is declared by tradition to be defeated and liable to punishment. (2.16)
When witnesses exist on both sides, the witnesses belong to the plaintiff; but when the initial claim has been refuted, they belong to the defendant. (2.17)
If the dispute should involve a wager, he shall cause the loser to pay the fine, his own stake, and the debt itself to the creditor. (2.18)
Setting aside deception, the king should conduct legal proceedings according to the facts;
for even a fact, if not presented, is lost in a lawsuit. (2.19)

One who denies a written document when even one part of it is proven, shall be made by the king to pay all the amounts in dispute; however, he must not be made to pay what was not previously claimed. 2.20.
When there is a conflict between Smṛti and Nyāya, the latter prevails in legal proceedings;
however, Dharmaśāstra is more authoritative than Arthaśāstra—this is the established rule. (2.21)
Written documents, possession, and witnesses are declared to be the means of proof.
In the absence of any one of these, one of the divine ordeals is prescribed. (2.22)
In all disputes whatsoever, the subsequent legal act is stronger;
however, in the case of a mortgage, a gift, or a purchase, the prior act is more powerful. (2.23)
For one who sees land being enjoyed by another but does not speak out, there is loss after twenty years; for wealth, the loss occurs after ten years. //2.24//
Except for property placed within boundary lines, deposits, and the wealth of the mentally dull or children;
likewise, except for bailments, the property of the king, women, and Vedic scholars. (2.25)

For one who steals deposits and the like, the king shall cause the thief to pay the wealth to the owner, as well as a fine equal to that amount to the king, or otherwise according to his capacity. ||2.26||
Title-deed is superior to possession, except when it has come down through prior succession;
even a title-deed has no strength at all where there is not even the slightest possession.
But he by whom the title-deed was executed shall, when summoned, produce it;
neither his son nor his grandson need do so, for in that case possession is more weighty.
Possession attains the status of valid proof through pure title;
possession based on impure title does not attain validity. (2.29)
If one who has been accused should have passed away, his heir shall clear him of that charge;
in such a case, possession does not constitute proof without a legal title. (2.30)

In the legal procedure for men, the king, the officials in charge of affairs, guilds, trade associations, and then families—each preceding one is to be known as more authoritative than the following. (2.31)
He shall set aside legal proceedings brought about by force or fraud, as well as those conducted at night, within the inner apartments, outside the home, or instigated by enemies. (2.32)
A legal proceeding initiated by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by disease, distressed, a child, or terrified, as well as one that is unrelated [to the facts], is not valid. (2.33)
Having disciplined families, castes, guilds, assemblies, and even districts that have strayed from their own duty, the king shall establish them on the right path.
Property lost and subsequently recovered must be returned by the king to the owner;
if he cannot prove his ownership by signs, he deserves a fine equal to its value.
Having found a treasure, the king should give half to the twice-born;
the learned twice-born, however, may take the whole, since he is the master of everything. (2.36)
When a treasure has been found by another, the king shall take a sixth part;
if it is discovered without having been reported, he shall be made to pay that [the full amount] as well as a fine.
The king must restore property stolen by thieves to the people; for by not restoring it, he incurs the same guilt as the one to whom it belongs. (2.38)
With a pledge, the interest shall be one-eightieth part every month;
otherwise, according to the order of the castes, it shall be two, three, four, or five percent per hundred. (2.39)
The interest on the value of livestock and female slaves is eightfold; likewise, that on clothes, grain, and gold is fourfold, threefold, and twofold respectively. (2.40)

But those who travel through forests shall pay ten percent, and those who travel by sea shall pay twenty percent or a hundred percent; or all [creditors] may take the interest agreed upon by themselves, regardless of the species of the debtors. (2.41)
One who is proving the case for a plaintiff shall not be censured by the king;
but if he fails while the case is being proved, he shall go before the king, be punished, and be made to pay that wealth. (2.42)
A debtor should pay the creditors according to the order in which they were approached;
however, he should first pay the Brāhmaṇa and immediately thereafter the king. (2.43)
The king shall compel the debtor to pay ten percent on the amount recovered;
however, the creditor who has obtained his money shall be made to pay five percent.
One may compel a man of low birth who has become impoverished to perform labor for the sake of repaying a debt;
however, a Brāhmaṇa who is impoverished should be made to pay gradually, according to his income. 2.45.
If one's own wealth that has been lent out is not accepted when it is being returned, it shall remain deposited with a neutral third party; it does not increase beyond that point.

The son of a woman who took a loan shall pay that debt, as shall the son of a woman who took a pledge; likewise, a son whose property is not dependent on others shall pay for his father who died intestate. (2.47)
Whatever debt may have been contracted for the sake of the family by those who are undivided, the heirs shall pay it when the head of the household has died or gone abroad. (2.48)
A wife shall not pay a debt incurred by her husband or son, nor shall a father pay one incurred by his son;
likewise, a husband shall not pay a debt incurred by his wife, except for the sake of the family. (2.49)
The husband shall pay the debt of a cowherd’s wife, a liquor-seller’s wife, an actress’s wife, a washerwoman’s wife, or a hunter’s wife, because their livelihood depends upon him. 2.50.
A woman shall pay a debt incurred by her husband with her consent, or one contracted jointly with him, or even one contracted by herself; she is not liable for any other debt. (2.51)
When the father has gone abroad, is deceased, or is overwhelmed by calamity, the debt must be paid by the sons or grandsons; if it is denied, it is established by witnesses. (2.52)
A son shall not pay, on behalf of his father, debts incurred through liquor, lust, gambling, fines, or taxes, nor what remains unpaid after such deductions, nor any gift made for no purpose. (2.53)

Furthermore, it is declared in the Smṛti that among brothers, between husband and wife, and between father and son, suretyship, debt, and witness testimony do not apply when they have not separated their property. (2.54)
Suretyship is ordained for appearance, for testimony, and for payment;
however, in the event of failure, the first two must pay, and in the case of the latter, even the sons must pay. (2.55)

Where a guarantor for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a guarantor for confidence (*prātyayika*) has died, their sons shall not pay the debt; however, those who stood as sureties for payment (*dāna*) must pay it. (2.56)
If there were many guarantors, they should repay the debt with their own respective shares; however, when they stand under a single liability, the creditor may collect from them as he pleases. (2.57)
Where a surety has been compelled to pay the debt publicly to the creditor, that money must be repaid by the debtors to him at double the amount. (2.58)
Grain that includes its offspring and is suitable for cattle and goats shall be repaid threefold;
clothing shall be given fourfold, and liquids likewise eightfold. (2.59)
A pledge shall be forfeited when the debt has doubled, provided it is not redeemed;
however, a pledge for a fixed term expires at the end of that time, whereas a pledge to be enjoyed for its produce is never forfeited.

When a deposit consisting of a cow or other animal has been used, no interest shall accrue; likewise, no interest is due when a beneficial pledge (sopakāra) has been enjoyed or when its value has been depreciated.
If the object is lost or destroyed by an act of God or the king, it need not be replaced, except in cases caused by negligence. (2.61)

Once the pledge is established through its formal acceptance, even if it is being protected, if it reaches a state of worthlessness, another pledge or the principal sum itself must be delivered to the creditor. (2.62)
One shall cause the debtor to pay the money secured by a pledge for conduct along with interest;
