however, one shall cause the value of a deposit made under a verbal agreement to be returned doubled.
When the time for repayment has arrived, the pledge must be released; otherwise, the debtor shall be fined.
If there is no one to act as the intermediary, the creditor may deposit the money with a local family and take possession of the pledge. (2.64)
Or it may remain there at the value fixed at that time, without interest;
or, with the consent of the debtor, he may sell it in the presence of witnesses. (2.65)

But when the debt has become doubled, then indeed the pledge must be released once the money produced from it has entered [the creditor's possession] and reached the amount of double [the original loan]. (2.66)

When an object contained in a vessel is handed over into another's hand without being specifically described, that property is termed *aupanidhika* (a sealed deposit); it must be returned in exactly the same condition. ||2.67||
But he shall not be made to pay for what has been stolen by the king, by fate, or by thieves;
however, if it is lost when he fails to return it upon being asked, he shall be made to pay for it and a fine equal to its value. ||2.68||
One who lives by his own will shall be punished and made to pay that [debt] along with interest;
this same rule applies to borrowed goods, items held in trust, deposits, and pledges. (2.69)
Ascetic, charitable by nature, of noble birth, truthful, devoted primarily to dharma, upright, blessed with sons, and endowed with wealth. ||2.70||

Witnesses should be known as at least three in number, devoted to the performance of the five great sacrifices; they may be of the same caste and class as the parties, or all may be eligible for all classes. (2.71)
Women, the elderly, children, gamblers, those intoxicated, the insane, the accused, performers on stage, heretics, forgers, and those with impaired faculties; 2.72.

An outcast, a relative, one interested in the matter, an associate, an enemy, a thief, one who commits violence, one whose fault has been observed, and one who has been expelled—these are not competent witnesses. (2.73)
Even a single person who knows the law may be a witness if he is approved by both parties;
however, in cases of adultery, theft, verbal abuse, and violence, everyone may be a witness. (2.74)
For if men do not testify regarding a debt along with its tenfold interest,
the king shall cause the debtor to pay the entire amount on the forty-sixth day.
For that lowest of men who does not give testimony even though he knows [the facts] is indeed equal to false witnesses in both his sin and his punishment. (2.76)
He should cause the witnesses, who stand in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant, to hear [the following]:
"Those worlds which belong to those who commit minor sins, as well as those belonging to the perpetrators of the great sins..."
Whatever worlds belong to those who set fire to dwellings and those who kill women and children—all of those he attains who gives false testimony. (2.78)
Whatever merit you have performed throughout hundreds of previous births, know that it all belongs to him whom you defeat through falsehood. (2.79)

In a conflict between witnesses, the testimony of the majority prevails; likewise, when they are equal in number, that of those possessing superior qualities; but when there is a conflict even among those of superior qualities, the statement of those who possess the most excellent qualities should be accepted. 2.80.
He whose witnesses declare his claim to be true shall be the victor;
he who speaks otherwise shall certainly suffer defeat. (2.81)
Even when testimony has been given by witnesses, if others who are more virtuous or twice as numerous should state it otherwise, the former witnesses shall be considered perjured. (2.82)
The forger and likewise the witnesses shall each be punished separately;
they shall forfeit property equal to twice the value of the dispute, and a Brāhmaṇa offender shall be banished.

He who, being made to hear the testimony by another, denies it while shrouded in darkness, shall be compelled to pay eight times the value of the property; however, in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, he shall be banished. 2.84.
But where the execution of those belonging to the [first three] castes would occur, there one may speak untruth as testimony;
to purify that [act], the twice-born should offer a *caru* oblation to Sarasvatī. (2.85)
Whatever matter has been settled by mutual agreement through their own consent, a document should be executed regarding it, containing witnesses and beginning with the name of the creditor. (2.86)
It should be marked with the year, month, half-month, day, time, birth, and lineage; and with the name of one's fellow student, oneself, and one's father. (2.87)
When the matter is concluded, the debtor shall write his own name by his own hand:
"What is written above is approved by me, the son of so-and-so. (2.88)
And the witnesses, preceded by the names of their fathers, should write with their own hands: "I, so-and-so, am a witness here"; thus they should be written down, being unequal in number. (2.89)
He who is illiterate or a debtor should cause his own statement to be written down, either by himself or by another witness, in the presence of all the witnesses. (2.90)
"Having been requested by both parties, this has been written by me, the son of so-and-so, named so-and-so"; thus should the scribe write at the end. (2.91)
Even without witnesses, a document written in one's own hand is declared to be valid as evidence in its entirety, except when it was produced through force or fraud. (2.92)
A debt recorded in a document must be paid by only three generations of men; however, a pledge is enjoyed only so long as that debt has not been repaid. (2.93)
If a document is located in another country, is difficult to read, lost, rubbed out, stolen, torn,
broken, or burnt, one should have another document executed.

That which is written by one's own hand for the purpose of clarifying a doubtful meaning [is authoritative], by means of reasoning, attainment, performance, signs, connection, scripture, and logical grounds. (2.95)
The creditor shall write on the back of the document what has been received from the debtor;
or he may give a receipt, signed with his own hand, for what has been paid. (2.96)
Having paid the debt, one should tear up the document, or for the sake of purification, have another one executed;
and that which was executed with witnesses must be repaid in the presence of witnesses. (2.97)

The balance, fire, water, poison, and the sacred libation (kośa) are the ordeals for the purpose of purification in this world; these are used in cases of grave accusation when the accuser has placed his head [as a stake]. 2.98.
Or, by mutual consent, one may perform [the role] while the other serves as the head;
even without a formal head, one may act in cases of treason against the king or in the event of a mortal sin.
In legal proceedings concerning matters of state, those who are pure shall always employ the ploughshare, the balance, and the poison, but never for more than one thousand [paṇas]. (2.100)
For a value of a thousand, one should cause the balance and other ordeals to be performed; even for a small amount, one should have the ordeal conducted.
One who is pure shall be made to pay fifty [paṇas]; one who is impure shall be subject to punishment. ||2.101||
Having summoned one who has fasted since sunrise and bathed with his clothes on, he should cause all the ordeals to be performed in the presence of the king and Brāhmaṇas. (2.102)
For women, children, the elderly, the afflicted, the lame, Brahmins, and the sick, the ordeal shall be by balance;
for a Śūdra, by fire or water; or for seven barley grains in the case of poison. (2.103)
The man mounted upon the balance was examined by experts skilled in weighing; once he had been made equal to the counterweight, the lines were marked and he was lowered. (2.104)
O Tula, you were created of old by the gods as the abode of truth;
therefore, speak the truth, O auspicious one, and release me from my doubt.
"If I am a doer of evil, O Mother, then lead me downward;
if I am pure, lead me upward"—thus one should consecrate the scale. (2.106)
Then, having observed that the hands have been rubbed with rice grains,
one should place seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree upon them and wrap them with a thread for that same duration.
O Agni, Purifier, you move within all beings;
O Sage, like a witness, speak the truth to me regarding my merits and sins. 2.108
When he has spoken thus, one should quickly place fifty palas of even iron, heated to the color of fire, upon both of his hands.
Taking that [measuring cord], he should slowly walk seven mandalas;
each mandala should be known to be sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in extent, with an equal interval between them. ||2.110||
If the fire is extinguished, or if the grain is crushed but not burnt, he attains purification; if the sacrificial ball falls midway, or if there is doubt, he should perform the rite again. (2.111)
Having sworn an oath with the words, "O Varuṇa,
protect me by truth," he should take hold of the thighs of one standing in water reaching up to the navel and enter the water.
If a swift man could bring back an arrow shot at that same moment, and if, after the other has departed, he should see the body submerged, he would obtain purification. (2.113)
O Poison, son of Brahmā, established in the dharma of truth, protect us from this curse; by virtue of your truthfulness, become nectar for me.
Having spoken thus, one should consume the Śārṅga poison born of the snowy mountains;
when it is digested without its characteristic effects, one should declare that person purified.
Having worshipped the fierce deities, one should take their bathing water;
having made [the patient] hear [mantras], one should then cause him to drink three handfuls of that water. (2.116)
If a terrible calamity, whether caused by the king or by fate, befalls us within fourteen days, he shall be proven innocent; of this there is no doubt. (2.117)
If the father should make a partition, he may divide the sons according to his will; either he may give the eldest a superior share, or all may be equal sharers. (2.118)
If he should give equal shares, the wives whose woman’s property (*strīdhana*) was not given by the husband or by the father-in-law must be made sharers of an equal portion. (2.119)
If one who is capable does not desire [to divide], then after giving something [to him], a separate arrangement is made;
this is remembered as the law established by the father for those whose shares are deficient or excessive.
After the death of both parents, the sons shall divide the inheritance and the debt equally.
The daughters shall take the remainder of the mother's estate after the debts have been cleared; in their absence, the succession goes to the [mother's] lineage.
Whatever else is acquired by oneself without the depletion of the paternal estate, as well as what is obtained through friendship or marriage, shall not belong to the heirs. (2.122)
When the property arises as a common whole, the division is traditionally held to be equal;
however, for those who have multiple fathers, the allotment of shares is determined according to the fathers. (2.123)
Whether it be land acquired by the grandfather, or a hereditary grant, or even property itself—in all such cases, the ownership of both father and son shall be equal. (2.124)

A son born after the property has been divided is entitled to a share from his mother’s estate; or rather, his share shall be determined from the visible assets, after deducting all income and expenses. (2.125)
If one recovers property that was taken and had come into his possession by succession, he need not give it to the co-heirs; the same applies to what has been acquired through learning. (2.126)
Whatever has been given by both parents shall belong to that [child] alone.
After the father's death, when they divide [the estate], the mother also shall receive an equal share. (2.127)

But those who have not yet been consecrated should be consecrated by their brothers who have already been consecrated; and the sisters, having received a fourth part from their own share, [are likewise to be consecrated]. (2.128)
The sons of a Brāhmaṇa, according to their respective castes, receive four, three, two, and one shares;
those born of a Kṣatriya receive three, two, and one shares; and the two born of a Vaiśya receive two and one shares. (2.129)
If property that was taken from one another by those who have already divided their inheritance is later discovered, they shall divide it again into equal shares; such is the settled rule. (2.130)
A son begotten by appointment upon the wife of a man who has no son is,
according to the law, the heir to the estate and the giver of the funeral oblation for both fathers.

The legitimate son is one born of a lawful wife; equal to him is the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra). The son of the field (kṣetraja) is one begotten by a kinsman of the same lineage or by another. (2.132)
A son born secretly in the house is considered a *gūḍhaja* (secret-born) son;
a son born of an unmarried girl is considered a *kānīna* (maiden-born) son, the son of his maternal grandfather. ||2.133||
A son born of a woman who has been previously married, whether she was still a virgin or not, is a *paunarbhava*.
A son whom either the mother or the father gives away becomes a *dattaka* (given son). (2.134)
One who is purchased from those two is a "purchased" son; one made by oneself is an "artificial" (kṛtrima) son;
one who has given himself is a "self-given" (svayandatta) son; and one conceived in the womb and discovered [there] is a "son received with the bride" (sahoḍhaja). (2.135)
But he who is taken up after being abandoned becomes an *apaviddha* son;
among these, the one who follows each preceding one in the absence of the former provides the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) and inherits the share. (2.136)

This rule has been declared by me for sons born of wives of the same caste; however, even one born of a Śūdra woman through a Śūdra husband shall, if born of desire, be a sharer of the inheritance. (2.137)
When the father has died, the brothers shall make him a sharer of half [the estate];
one who has no brothers shall take everything, except for the son of a daughter. (2.138)
The wife, the daughters, the parents, the brothers, as well as their sons, a kinsman of the same lineage, a relative, a pupil, and fellow students; ||2.139||
In the absence of these, each subsequent one among them is the heir to the wealth of the deceased who left no son; for this rule applies to all castes. (2.140)
The heirs of forest-dwellers, ascetics, and students are, respectively: the teacher, the virtuous pupil, the spiritual brother, and one who shares the same sacred site (tīrtha). (2.141)
But a reunited coparcener shall give and take the share of one who was reunited, as well as of a uterine brother; this applies both to one born after reunion and to one who dies before it. (2.142)

A uterine brother who is a reunited coparcener shall take the wealth, not a non-uterine brother; even one who is not reunited shall take it if he is uterine, but not one born of a different mother. (2.143)
His son who is an outcaste, impotent, lame, insane, idiotic, blind, or afflicted by an incurable disease shall be maintained, but they are entitled to no share of the inheritance. (2.144)
But their sons born of their own wives (aurasa-kṣetraja) are entitled to a share and are free from fault;
and their daughters must be maintained until they are given away to husbands. (2.145)
The childless wives among them who are of virtuous conduct should be maintained; however, those who are unchaste as well as those who are hostile should be banished. (2.146)

That which is given by her father, mother, husband, or brothers; that which is received before the nuptial fire; and that which is given upon supersession—this is declared to be a woman’s property (strīdhana). // 2.147 //
The property given by the father-in-law, as well as the nuptial fee and the subsequent gift—these, upon the death of a childless woman, her kinsmen shall obtain. (2.148)
The property of a woman who dies without issue belongs to her husband even in the case of the four [forms of marriage] beginning with the Brāhma;
however, among the remaining [forms], if she has daughters who have borne children, that property goes to the father. (2.149)
Having given away his daughter, he who takes her back shall be punished and made to pay the expenses along with interest;
if she has died, he may take back what was given after deducting the expenses incurred by both parties. (2.150)
In times of famine, for the sake of religious duties, during illness, or when there is an obstruction, a husband is not required to give back to his wife the property she received from him. (2.151)

If he marries another wife, he shall give to the first wife an equal amount as compensation for her supersession; however, if no separate property was given to her, half of that amount is prescribed. (2.152)
In a denial of partition, [proof is established] by kinsmen, relatives, witnesses, and documents;
and by the manifestation of partition through the receipt of shares, houses, fields, and dowries. ||2.153||
In a dispute concerning the boundary of a field, the neighbors, elders, village assemblies, cowherds, farmers, and all others who frequent the forest shall [decide]. (2.154)
They should establish the boundary at its limit, characterized by landmarks such as ground, charcoal, husks, trees, embankments, anthills, depressions, bones, shrines, and so forth. (2.155)
Or four, eight, or ten neighboring kings from the entire assembly, wearing red garlands and garments, shall lead the boundary-markers to the boundary. (2.156)
But those who speak falsely shall be punished separately by the king with the middle amercement;
in the absence of witnesses and signs, the king is the establisher of the boundary. (2.157)
This same rule should be understood to apply to groves, temples, villages, water-reservoirs, gardens, and houses, as well as to the flow of rainwater. (2.158)
In the case of breaking a boundary, as well as in the seizure of a field, and for the transgression of a limit, there are indeed punishments of the lowest, highest, and middle degrees. (2.159)
A dam that causes little harm and brings about prosperity should not be prohibited;
a well that yields much water may take up a small portion of another's field. (2.160)
If one constructs an irrigation channel on a field without having informed the owner, the produce belongs to the owner; in his absence, it belongs to the king. (2.161)

If one neither cultivates nor causes to be cultivated a field that has already been ploughed, the king shall make him pay the value of the crop that was harvested and cause another to cultivate the field. (2.162)
A buffalo that destroys standing crops shall be fined eight māṣas;
a cow, half of that; and a goat or sheep, half of that again. (2.163)
For those who remain after having eaten, the fine is double; for those who stay overnight, it is likewise.
This same rule applies even in a pasture, as does the penalty for a donkey or camel, which is equal to that for a buffalo.

As long as the crop is destroyed, so long shall the owner of the field receive the fruit [of his loss]; however, the herdsman shall be beaten, while the owner of the cattle deserves the previously mentioned fine. (2.165)
There is no offense in [entering] a field located at the edge of a path, a village, or a pasture, provided it is unintentional;
if done intentionally, one deserves punishment like that of a thief. (2.166)

A bull that has been set free, cattle that have lost their keeper, a cow that has recently calved, one that is newly pregnant, and those whose herdsman is overwhelmed by divine calamity or the king—these must be released from liability for damage. (2.167)
Just as a cowherd should return the cattle entrusted to him in the evening, so too must one who has received wages be made to pay for those that have died or been lost through negligence. (2.168)
But when damage occurs through the fault of the keeper, a fine is prescribed for the keeper:
twelve and a half paṇas, and the value of the property must be paid to the owner. (2.169)
With the consent of the village, or by royal decree, a twice-born man may take grass, firewood, and flowers from anywhere as if they were his own. (2.170)
The distance between a village and its field shall be one hundred bow-lengths;
that for a market town (karvaṭa) shall be two hundred, and for a city (nagara), four hundred. (2.171)
One shall recover one's own property sold by another; the fault lies with the purchaser if the sale was not publicly announced.
One who buys from a low person in secret for a low price at an improper time is a thief. (2.172)
Having recovered property that was lost or stolen, one should cause the thief to be apprehended;
or, if there is a lapse of time or place, one should seize the person oneself and hand him over. (2.173)
Purification comes from seeing the seller; the owner recovers the property, the king receives a fine, and the buyer recovers his price from whoever was the seller there. (2.174)
What has been lost must be recovered through legal title and possession; otherwise, there is a fine of five times the value, and the king incurs a penalty for failing to restore it. (2.175)
He who recovers property that has been stolen or lost from the hand of another, without having reported it to the king, shall be fined ninety-six paṇas. (2.176)
If property that was lost or stolen is recovered by customs officers or local guards, the owner shall recover it within one year; after that period, the king shall take it. (2.177)
For killing a single-hoofed animal, one should pay five paṇas; for a human, four;
for buffaloes, camels, and cows, two each; and for goats and sheep, one-quarter each. (2.178)

One may give away property without detriment to one's own family, except for one's wife and sons; however, when there is a lineage remaining, one’s entire estate must not be given, nor that which is dependent on another. (2.179)
The acceptance [of a gift] should be public, especially in the case of immovable property;
and what has been promised as a gift must be given, and once given, one must not take it back again.
The examination of seeds, iron, draft animals, gems, women, milch cattle, and men shall take ten days, one day, five days, seven days, one month, three days, and half a month respectively. (2.181)
Gold is not diminished when placed in fire; silver [loses] two palas per hundred;
but lead and tin [lose] eight, and copper five, while iron [loses] ten.
In a hundred [palas], there is an increase of ten palas for woolen and likewise for cotton cloth;
in the medium quality, there is a decrease of five palas, while in the fine quality, a decrease of three palas is prescribed. (2.183)
In the case of leather and hair-cloth, a loss of one-thirtieth is recognized;
however, there shall be neither loss nor increase in the case of silk or bark-cloth.

Having ascertained the place, the time, and the nature of the enjoyment, as well as the strength and weakness of the lost goods, those who are experts shall declare what must be paid; that [the debtor] shall undoubtedly be made to pay. (2.185)
One who has been forcibly enslaved by thieves, as well as one who has been sold, is liberated by providing for his master's life, or by being adopted, or even by the payment of a ransom. (2.186)
One who has been expelled from the order of renunciation becomes the king’s slave for life; among the social classes, servitude may be according to the natural order, but never against it. (2.187)

Even when he has mastered the craft, the apprentice should remain in the teacher's house for the prescribed period; having received his food from the teacher, he shall offer the fruits of his labor to him. (2.188)
Having established a settlement in the city and settled the Brāhmaṇas there, the king should provide for those learned in the three Vedas and say: "Let your own duty be protected. (2.189)
But that which is conventional and does not conflict with one's own dharma, as well as that dharma established by the king, must also be protected with effort. (2.190)
But he who misappropriates the property of the community, or he who violates a formal agreement, the king shall confiscate all his possessions and banish him from the realm. (2.191)
The advice of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be followed by all;
whoever acts contrary to that shall be made to pay the first fine. (2.192)

The lord of the earth, having honored those who have come for the sake of the community's business with gifts, marks of respect, and hospitality, should dismiss them once their business has been accomplished. (2.193)
One who has been dispatched for the business of a collective shall hand over whatever he may obtain;
if he does not hand it over himself, he shall be made to pay eleven times that amount. (2.194)
Those who are knowers of the Vedas, pure, and free from greed should be the deliberators of affairs;
the word of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be carried out. (2.195)
This same rule applies to guilds, merchant corporations, and groups of heretics;
the king should protect them from internal dissension and preserve their traditional livelihoods. (2.196)
If one who has received wages abandons his work, he shall pay double the amount;
if he has not received wages, the work shall be made equal [to the value of the wages], and the tools must be maintained by the servants.
But he who employs laborers without having fixed their wages must be made by the king to pay a tenth part of the profits from trade, cattle, or crops. (2.198)
If one should neglect the place and the time, or perform the work otherwise than required, in that case it shall be at the master's pleasure; if more has been done, more should be paid. (2.199)

Whatever amount of work one performs, for that much shall be his wages; provided there is no deceit on the part of either party, but in case of deceit, [the wage] shall be according to what was actually done. (2.200)
The carrier shall be made to pay for goods lost through no fault of the king or fate;
likewise, one who causes an obstruction to the departure shall be made to pay double the wages. (2.201)

If he abandons him on the way, he shall forfeit a seventh part of the fare at the start and a fourth on the road; if he abandons him halfway, he shall be made to pay the entire fare, and the deserter as well.
The keeper of the gambling house, however, may take five percent from a fraudulent gambler as his fee, but ten percent from any other. (2.203)
Having protected it properly, he should give the king the share as prescribed;
he should cause the winner to take what has been won and give it to the victor, being truthful in speech and patient. (2.204)

When the king's share has been obtained and the assembly of gamblers is well-known, one should cause the winner to pay the stake in a place where a court is present; otherwise, however, one should not.

For they alone are the observers of legal proceedings and the witnesses; therefore, those who play with fraudulent dice or by means of deception should be branded with a mark and banished by the king. (2.206)

Gambling should be conducted with a single stake for the purpose of identifying thieves; this same rule is to be understood as applying to betting on living creatures and to challenges to combat. (2.207)

If one insults those who are deficient in limbs, those with impaired senses, or those afflicted by disease, by means of praise that is true, false, or otherwise, he shall be fined twelve and a half paṇas. (2.208)
If a man swears, "I shall violate your sister or your mother," the king shall cause him to pay a fine of twenty-five [paṇas]. (2.209)

Half [of the standard fine] shall be imposed for offenses against those of lower status, double for women of others, and likewise for those of higher status; the application of punishment must be determined according to the relative superiority or inferiority of caste and class. (2.210)
In cases of slander against those of lower rank, the fines are four, three, and two times [the base amount] respectively;
for those of higher rank, they decrease by half from that same starting point in the reverse order.
In cases of verbal defamation involving the arms, neck, eyes, or thighs, the punishment is a fine of one hundred [paṇas];
for the feet, nose, ears, hands, and so forth, it is half of that. (2.212)
But one who is unable [to pay] and speaks thus shall be fined ten paṇas;
likewise, one who is able shall be made to provide a surety for his security. (2.213)
For an accusation made regarding an offense involving loss of caste (pātaniya), one should be punished with the middle amercement;
but for one involving a minor offense (upapātaka), he should be made to pay the first amercement. ||2.214||

For the three types of learned men, kings, and gods, the fine is the highest amercement; for guilds of castes, it is the middle amercement; and for villages and districts, it is the first amercement. (2.215)

But when a person has been killed without witnesses, the legal case must be investigated by means of physical marks, logical reasoning, and scriptural tradition, out of fear that false evidence might have been fabricated. (2.216)
A fine of ten paṇas is prescribed for touching [another] with ashes, mud, or dust;
for touching [another] with impure matter, the heel, or spittle, the fine is double that amount.
In the case of women who are equal [in status], the punishment is the same; for those of higher status, it is double;
for those of lower status, it is half; and there is no punishment if [the act] was committed through delusion, intoxication, and so forth. (2.218)
But a limb that causes pain to a Brahmin may be cut off from one who is not a Brahmin;
however, if he merely raised his weapon, the first amercement shall be the punishment, and half of that if he merely touched him. (2.219)
If hands or feet are raised [in a threatening manner], the fines shall be ten and twenty [paṇas] respectively;
but for all [such acts] against one another with a weapon, the middle amercement shall be imposed. (2.220)
For pulling at the feet, hair, or garment, or for seizing the hands, the fine shall be ten paṇas;
for causing pain, dragging, twisting, or placing the foot upon another, the punishment shall be one hundred [paṇas]. (2.221)
A man who inflicts pain with wood or other implements without drawing blood shall be made to pay a fine of thirty paṇas; if blood is seen, the fine shall be double. (2.222)
In the case of breaking a hand, foot, or tooth; in cutting off the ears or the nose;
in piercing a wound; and likewise in striking one who is nearly dead, the middle amercement is the punishment. (2.223)
In cases of obstructing movement, food, or speech; piercing the eyes or other [senses];
or breaking the neck, arms, or thighs, the punishment is the highest amercement. (2.224)
But for many who strike one person, the fines shall be double those as previously stated;
that which was taken during a quarrel must be restored, and the fine shall be double that amount. (2.225)
He who causes injury shall be made to pay the expenses incurred for its recovery, as well as the fine prescribed for that particular type of quarrel. (2.226)
A ferryman taking toll for goods transported over land shall be made to pay ten paṇas as a fine;
the same applies to a Brāhmaṇa who fails to invite his neighbors [to a feast]. (2.227)
In cases of striking, piercing, cutting, or causing a wall to collapse,
one shall be made to pay five, ten, or twenty paṇas, as well as the cost of the damage.
One who throws into a house property that causes suffering or is life-threatening shall be made to pay sixteen paṇas as a fine in the first instance, and double that amount in the second. (2.229)
In the case of causing pain, drawing blood, or likewise severing a branch or a limb, the fine for small animals shall be two paṇas and upwards in successive order. (2.230)
In the case of cutting off the male organ or killing [the animal], the middle amercement shall be imposed, as well as its value;
for these great animals, the fines at these places are double.
For the cutting of sprouts, twigs, branches, trunks, or entire trees that provide sustenance, the fine shall be twenty times twice [the standard], that is, forty-fold. 2.232.
In the case of trees grown at a shrine, a cemetery, a boundary, a holy place, or in a king's palace, as well as for a tree of renown, the fines are double. (2.233)
For the cutting of shrubs, clusters, bushes, creepers, spreading plants, medicinal herbs, and climbing vines, the fine shall be half of that prescribed for the previously mentioned places. (2.234)
Taking the property of another by force, whether in the presence of witnesses or through stealth, is declared to be *sāhasa* (violence).
The fine for this is twice the value of the object; however, if the accused denies it, the fine is fourfold. (2.235)
He who causes a rash act to be committed shall be made to pay double the fine;
but he who, having said "I will give," causes it to be done, shall pay four times the amount. (2.236)

One who offers water for honor (arghya) while using abusive language, one who transgresses [the bounds of propriety], one who strikes his brother’s wife, one who fails to deliver a message as instructed, and one who breaks down a house situated by the sea; ||2.237||
For those who cause harm to neighbors, kinsmen, and others, the settled rule is that their fine shall be fifty paṇas. (2.238)

One who approaches a widow against her will, one who does not run to the aid of someone crying out for help, one who raises a cry of distress without cause, and a Caṇḍāla who touches those of the highest caste—[these shall be punished]. 2.239.
One who feeds Śūdras or renunciants at rites for the gods or the ancestors; one who takes an improper oath; and one who performs the duties of an unfit person—[these are excluded]. (2.240)
One who obstructs the virility of bulls or small animals, one who denies a common property, and one who causes the destruction of a maidservant's fetus; 2.241.

Father and son, sister and brother, husband and wife, teacher and pupil: he who abandons any of these, provided they have not lost their caste status through a grave sin, shall be subject to a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. (2.242)
A washerman who wears another's garment shall be made to pay three *paṇas*;
if he sells, exchanges, pledges, or requests it [without permission], he shall pay ten *paṇas*. (2.243)
In cases such as a dispute between father and son, the fine for witnesses shall be two hundred;
and for anyone who stands as an intermediary between them, the fine shall also be eight hundred.
One who forges scales, royal edicts, measures, or coins, as well as anyone who deals with such forged items, shall be made to pay the highest fine. (2.245)
He who declares a counterfeit coin to be genuine, or a genuine coin to be counterfeit—that examiner of coins shall be made to pay the first amercement. (2.246)
A physician who practices falsely shall be made to pay the first fine for treating animals, the middle fine for treating humans, and the highest fine for treating those of royal status. (2.247)
He who binds one who should not be bound, or releases one who should be bound, and he who deals with one who is not of legal age, shall be made to pay the highest fine. (2.248)

Whoever should take even an eighth part [of the value] by means of false weights or scales, shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred; this penalty is prescribed for both increase and decrease [in the amount]. (2.249)
If one sells medicinal herbs, oils, salts, perfumes, grains, molasses, and other such goods by substituting inferior for superior quality, he shall be made to pay a fine of sixteen paṇas.

For the sale of clay, leather, gems, thread, iron, wood, bark, or cloth by one who does not belong to that class, the fine shall be eightfold for causing them to appear as if they belonged to that class. (2.251)
For one who brings for deposit or sale a casket containing counterfeit goods or artificial valuables, a punishment shall be prescribed. (2.252)
If the value is one paṇa, the fine is fifty; for one paṇa, it is said to be one hundred;
for two paṇas, the fine is two hundred; and as the price increases, the fine increases accordingly. (2.253)
For artisans and craftsmen who, acting together, fix a price that causes distress, a fine of one thousand [paṇas] is prescribed for every decrease or increase in that price. (2.254)
For merchants who, having banded together, withhold their merchandise at an improper price, or sell it [at such a price], the prescribed fine is the highest amercement (uttamasāhasa). ||2.255||
Whatever price is established for a commodity by the king, it is by that price that its sale or purchase is conducted;
from the surplus resulting therefrom, the profit of the merchants is ordained. (2.256)
A merchant who buys and sells immediately may take five percent on goods produced in his own country, but ten percent on those from a foreign land. (2.257)
Having deducted from the value of the merchandise the expenses incurred in producing it, a price should be fixed that is favorable to both the buyer and the seller. (2.258)

If one who has received the price does not deliver the merchandise to the buyer, he shall be made to pay it with interest; or, if the buyer has gone to another region, he shall be made to pay the profit derived from that region. (2.259)

Even after it has been sold, if the article remains to be sold because the previous buyer does not accept it, and if the loss is due to the fault of the buyer, that loss shall indeed belong to the buyer alone. (2.260)
If a defect arises in a commodity due to an injury caused by the king or fate, that loss belongs solely to the seller who, having been asked for it, does not deliver it. (2.261)
If, however, what has been sold into another's hand is defective, yet it is sold as if it were non-defective, the fine in that case shall be double its value. (2.262)
A merchant who understands the decrease and increase in value of commodities should not exercise regret after having purchased them; if he does so, he shall be liable to a fine of one-sixth.
When merchants perform work for the sake of profit through a partnership, the gain and loss shall be according to their respective capital, or as was agreed upon. (2.264)

If a deposit is lost through negligence—whether it was forbidden, not specifically instructed, or otherwise mishandled—the keeper shall restore it; furthermore, as its protector, he is entitled to a tenth part of its value. (2.265)
From the offering of the *argha* (tribute), the king shall take a twentieth part as duty;
that which is established by custom, what is fit for the king, and what has been sold [as such], belongs to the king. (2.266)
One who, departing from a customs station, falsely declares the quantity [of his goods], as well as one who buys or sells by deception, shall be made to pay eight times [the value]. (2.267)
When a deceased person has gone to another country, his heirs, kinsmen, or relatives shall take his property; if they have not arrived, the king shall take it. (2.268)
They should abandon that which is dishonest or profitless; one who is incapable should have it done by another.
By this rule, the duty of officiating priests, farmers, and laborers is declared.

A thief is apprehended by his captors either by means of stolen goods or by his footprints, or due to the offense of his prior actions; in the same way, one who dwells in impurity [is recognized]. (2.270)
Others also should be apprehended with suspicion on account of their concealment of caste, name, and so forth;
as well as those addicted to gambling, women, and liquor, and those whose faces and voices appear parched and altered. (2.271)

Those who inquire about the property and houses of others while moving about in secret, those who have no income yet have many expenditures, and those who sell goods that they do not possess—[these are spies]. (2.272)
If one who has been seized on suspicion of theft does not clear himself, he shall be made to restore the stolen property and be punished with the penalty for a thief. (2.273)
Having compelled the thief to restore what was stolen, the king shall have him executed by various means of corporal punishment;
however, having branded a Brāhmaṇa, he shall banish him from his own kingdom.

If cattle are killed or stolen, the fault lies with the village headman as long as they have not yet left the village; but on the road, it lies with the superintendent of the pasture-lands, or, if outside the pasture, with the one who fails to rescue them from thieves.
A village shall grant land within its own boundaries, or wherever it happens to go;
likewise, five villages or even ten villages may do so outside the cultivated area. (2.276)
Those who seize bandits, as well as those who steal horses and elephants, and those who kill by force, such men he shall cause to be impaled upon a stake. (2.277)
For the crimes of causing a monk to be expelled and breaking a sealed knot, the hands and nose should be cut off for the first offense;
for the second offense, one hand and one foot should be cut off.

In cases of seizing small, medium, or large property, punishment shall be determined according to its value; in the administration of legal penalties, one must carefully consider the place, time, age, and physical capacity [of the offender]. (2.279)
If one knowingly provides a thief or a murderer with food, shelter, fire, water, spells, or the means for their sustenance, the highest fine shall be imposed. (2.280)
For causing an abortion by striking with a weapon, the highest fine is prescribed;
likewise for the killing of a man or a woman, either the highest or the lowest fine applies. (2.281)
One who administers poison, a woman who kills her husband,
and one who destroys an embankment— these should be bound with stones and cast into the water, provided they are not pregnant.
One who administers poison or sets fire, or who causes the death of her husband, her teacher, or her own child,
should have her ears, hands, nose, and lips cut off and then be put to death by cows.
When someone has been killed while unobserved, his sons and kinsmen should be questioned immediately;
so too should his wives, who may be secretly attached to other men, be interrogated individually.
Or, desiring to know about women, livelihoods, or wealth, or with whom he has departed, he should slowly question people regarding the vicinity of the place of death. (2.285)
Those who set fire to fields, houses, villages, forests, pastures, or threshing floors,
as well as one who has sexual intercourse with the king's wife, shall be burned by a fire of straw mats.
A man shall be apprehended for adultery if he is caught by the hair with another's wife, or if he is caught with signs of sexual passion, or if both parties admit it. (2.287)

If the offender belongs to the same caste, the highest fine shall be imposed; if he is of a lower caste, the middle fine; but if he is of a higher caste, men shall be subject to corporal punishment, while for women, the nose and so forth shall be cut off. (2.288)
Touching her girdle, breasts, upper garment, or navel; touching her hair; conversing with her at an improper place or time; and staying together with her [are grounds for censure]. (2.289)

A woman who has been forbidden [from such conduct] shall be fined one hundred [paṇas], and a man who commits it two hundred; if there was no prohibition for the two of them, their punishment shall be the same as in the case of adultery (saṃgrahaṇa). || 2.290 ||
If a man abducts an adorned maiden, he shall pay the highest fine; otherwise, the lowest.
However, if the offender is of the same caste, the fine is as prescribed; but in the case of abduction from a higher caste (prātilomya), death is ordained by law.
There is no offense in approaching women who are willing and submissive; otherwise, it is base.
But in the case of defiling them, the hand shall be cut off for a woman of high rank, and likewise, death for one of the highest rank. (2.292)
A woman who corrupts [another] shall be fined one hundred; but she who makes a false accusation shall be fined two hundred.
One who has sexual intercourse with cattle shall be fined one hundred, and for having intercourse with a low-caste woman or a cow, the middle amercement. (2.293)
For a man who has sexual intercourse with female slaves, female servants, or likewise with women who are not forbidden [to him], he shall be made to pay a fine of fifty paṇas. (2.294)
For approaching a slave woman by force, a fine of ten paṇas is prescribed;
if she is unwilling and there are many men involved, the fine is twelve paṇas for each individually.
For one who approaches a woman in a non-vaginal opening, or who urinates upon a man, the fine is twenty-four paṇas; the same applies for approaching a female ascetic.
But for approaching a woman of the lowest caste, one should brand him with the mark of a headless trunk and banish him;
likewise, a Śūdra who approaches a woman of the lowest caste shall become a member of that same caste. For a man of the highest caste approaching a woman of the lowest caste, there is death. (2.297)
Whoever writes a royal edict with omissions or additions, or who releases an adulterer or a thief, shall receive the highest punishment. (2.298)
One who defiles a Brāhmaṇa with forbidden food shall be punished with the highest amercement;
for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement; for a Vaiśya, the first amercement; and for a Śūdra, half of that. (2.299)
One who deals in counterfeit gold and one who sells forbidden meat shall have three limbs cut off and be made to pay the highest fine. (2.300)
There is no offense for one who says "do not go away" when a four-footed animal has been struck;
likewise, there is no offense for striking with wood, clods of earth, arrows, stones, or by means of hand-to-hand combat. (2.301)
If a carriage with its nose-rope severed, or likewise with its yoke broken, should cause injury by backing up, the owner incurs no fault. (2.302)

Even if capable of doing so, a master who fails to rescue those with horns or fangs shall be made to pay the first amercement; likewise, if he failed to do so when a cry for help was raised, he shall pay double.
One who addresses a paramour as a "thief" shall be made to pay a fine of five hundred;
if he releases him after having lived off his wealth, he shall pay that same amount multiplied eightfold.
One who speaks what is displeasing to the king, as well as one who reviles him, and likewise one who breaks his counsel—having cut out their tongues, he should banish them. (2.305)
The punishment for one who sells the limbs of a corpse, for one who strikes his teacher, and likewise for one who mounts the royal vehicle or throne, is the middle amercement. (2.306)
For one who pierces two eyes, for one who issues commands hostile to the king, and likewise for a Śūdra living as a Brāhmaṇa, the fine shall be eight hundred [paṇas]. (2.307)
But if, after having seen a case wrongly decided, the king should conduct a review, the members of the court, together with the victor, shall each be fined double the amount in dispute. (2.308)
If one should think "I am not defeated" when he has been defeated according to the rule, the judge, having defeated him again upon his return, shall cause him to pay double the fine. (2.309)
Whatever fine has been unjustly taken by a king, he should report it to Varuṇa and himself give it to the Brahmins multiplied thirtyfold.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Legal Procedure," in the Dharmaśāstra of Yājñavalkya.
The Chapter on Expiation (Prāyaścitta)
One should bury a child less than two years of age and should not offer water for them thereafter;
others who have died should be followed by their relatives as far as the cremation ground. (3.1)

If he has entered [the order], he should be cremated with the worldly fire by those reciting the Yama-sūkta and the Gāthās, according to the procedure for one who maintained the sacred fires, provided that purpose is fulfilled.
From the seventh or even the tenth generation, the kinsmen descend into the waters; facing the direction of the ancestors, they recite: "May our sin be burned away by this water. (3.3)
In this same manner, the water-offering rite (udakakriyā) is performed for maternal grandfathers and teachers;
however, the offering of water out of affection (kāmodaka) is for friends, sisters-in-law, maternal cousins, fathers-in-law, and officiating priests.
Restraining their speech, they should pour out water once, pronouncing the name and the lineage;
those who are students of sacred knowledge (brahmacārins) shall not perform this water-libation, nor shall those who are outcasts (patitas).

Those who have taken refuge in heresy, thieves, women who kill their husbands, those who go after their lusts, those who drink liquor, and those who commit suicide shall not partake in the impurity rites nor receive the water libations. (3.6)
When they have finished the water rites, emerged from the water, and are seated upon soft grass,
one should address those who have bathed with ancient historical narratives.
He who seeks a core in human existence—which is as pithless as the trunk of a plantain tree and resembles a bubble on the water—is utterly deluded. (3.8)
If this body, composed of five elements, has returned to its fivefold state, what cause for lamentation is there, since it was produced by the very actions arising from one's own body? (3.9)
The earth, the vehicle-bearer, shall go to destruction, as will the oceans and the deities;
how then shall the mortal world, which resembles foam, not go to destruction? (3.10)
Since the deceased, being powerless, must consume the phlegm and tears shed by his kinsmen, one should not weep; rather, funeral rites should be performed according to one's ability.
Having reflected thus, they should go home preceded by children;
having bitten neem leaves, they should remain restrained at the door of their house.
Having sipped water, they should then touch fire, water, cow dung, and white mustard seeds;
then, having touched them, they should enter, placing their feet slowly upon a stone.
They should eat what they have purchased or obtained and sleep separately on the ground; food should be offered to the deceased for three days according to the ritual procedure of the Piṇḍayajña.
Water should be kept for one day in the open air, and milk in an earthen vessel; furthermore, the ritual acts based on the Vaitānika fires must be performed, as seen in the Śruti. (3.15)
Even for those who have touched a corpse, the rites beginning with entry [into the village] are permitted;
for those who so desire, purification occurs instantly, while for others it comes through bathing and self-restraint. (3.16)
Even after carrying out the funeral rites for his teacher, sub-teacher, or father, one who is under a vow remains under that vow;
he should not eat food from a mat (or coarse food) nor dwell together with them.
The impurity due to death is said to last ten nights or three nights;
however, for a child under two years of age, it lasts for both [parents], while the impurity due to birth belongs to the mother alone. (3.18)
For a Brāhmaṇa, the impurity due to death lasts ten days;
for a Kṣatriya, twelve days; and for a Vaiśya, fifteen days. (3.19)
The period of impurity for a Śūdra on account of a death is said to be thirty days; if another birth or death occurs during that interval, he becomes pure after the remaining days. (3.20)

In the case of a miscarriage, the number of nights equal to the months [of gestation] is the cause of purification; if the husband has gone abroad, the remaining period [of the impurity] shall apply; when the full term has passed, one becomes pure after offering water libations. 3.21.

But for approaching unmarried girls, as well as children, a teacher, a pupil, a fellow student of the Veda, a maternal uncle, or a learned Śrotriya, the purification is that prescribed for a day. (3.22)
In the case of sons other than those of one's own body, when wives have gone to others,
and likewise when the king is the resident authority, that day is the cause for purification.

For those who have killed a cow, a king, or a Brahmin, for those who kill themselves, and for those who desire [death] by their own will through fasting, weapons, fire, poison, and so forth—the [impurity lasts] immediately. (3.24)
There is no period of impurity for kings who have been slain by lightning,
nor for those killed in battle for the sake of cows or Brahmins, nor for one whom the lord of the earth so desires.
A Brahmin must never follow a deceased Śūdra;
having followed him, however, he becomes pure by bathing in water, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter. (3.26)

As well as for officiating priests and those consecrated for the sacrificial rite while performing the ritual act, and likewise for those observing the vow of the three-night sacrifice, celibate students, donors, and knowers of Brahman.
In giving gifts, at a wedding, during a sacrifice, in battle, during a national calamity, and even in times of dire distress, immediate purification is ordained. (3.28)
Regarding the birth-impurity (sūtaka) of the parents, it certainly belongs to the mother because of the appearance of that blood;
on that day, however, there is no defilement for the ancestors, because of the cause of their own birth.

If he is touched by those who have had contact with a woman in her courses or by those who are impure from death or birth, he should bathe; if he is merely touched by them, he should sip water and mutter the Sāvitrī mantra once mentally, using verses containing the word "water."
Time, fire, action, earth, wind, mind, knowledge, austerity, water, remorse, and fasting—all these are causes of purification. (3.31)
For those who have committed improper acts, the giving of gifts is purifying; for a river, its current is purifying;
for that which is to be cleansed, earth and water are purifying; and for the twice-born, renunciation is indeed purifying. (3.32)

Austerity is said to be the strength of those who know the Vedas, forbearance that of the wise, water that of the body, silent recitation that of those whose sins are concealed, and truth that of the mind. (3.33)
For the elemental self (bhūtātman), austerity and knowledge are the means of purification; for the intellect (buddhi), it is wisdom (jñāna).
For the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), purification through the knowledge of the Lord (īśvara) is considered supreme. (3.34)

In times of distress, a twice-born man may live by the occupation of a Kshatriya, or even that of a Vaishya; but once he has emerged from that difficulty, having abandoned that means for the sake of wealth, he should purify himself and remain established on his own path.
Fruits, stones, linen, the Soma plant, humans, cakes, creepers, sesame, boiled rice, liquids, alkaline substances, curd, milk, ghee, and water. (3.36)
Weapons, liquor, beeswax, honey, lac, sacrificial grass, earth, leather, flowers, blankets made of goat hair, hair, buttermilk, poison, and eraka grass; 3.37.
Silk, indigo, salt, meat, one-hoofed animals, and their causes;
likewise vegetables, moist medicinal herbs, oil-cakes, cotton, and perfumes. (3.38)
Even while maintaining his livelihood through the occupation of a Vaiśya, he should never sell sesame seeds;
for the sake of dharma, sesame seeds may be exchanged for an equal amount of grain. (3.39)
Selling salt, lac, and daughter, as well as milk, curd, and liquor, are acts that cause one to fall; they indeed bring about a loss of caste. (3.40)
A Brahmin who, when fallen into distress, accepts or consumes food from anyone whatsoever, is not defiled by sin; for he is equal to fire and the sun.

Agriculture, craftsmanship, service for wages, learning, usury, a cart, the mountains, service to others, marshlands, and the king—along with begging—are the means of livelihood in times of distress. (3.42)
Having remained hungry for three days, one may take wealth from a non-Brāhmaṇa;
having received it, it must be reported according to the law by the person who was approached. (3.43)
Having ascertained his conduct, lineage, character, learning, and education, as well as his sons, the king shall provide for him a righteous livelihood from his own treasury.

Having formally settled his wife [in the household], or followed by her, he dwells in the forest as a forest-dweller (vānaprastha), observing celibacy (brahmacārī), maintaining the sacred fires along with the domestic fire (aupāsana), and remaining patient. (3.45)
One who maintains a beard and hair, who is self-possessed, should constantly satisfy with food grown without the plow the sacred fires, the ancestors, the gods, guests, and his dependents. (3.46)
One should accumulate wealth for the sake of a day, a month, six months, or likewise for a year; what has been accumulated should be spent in the month of Āśvayuja.
Self-controlled, bathing three times a day, abstaining from accepting gifts, devoted to sacred study, habitually generous, and intent on the welfare of all beings. (3.48)
Using his teeth as a mortar, eating only what is ripened by time, or using a stone for grinding,
he should perform the rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, as well as other ritual acts, with fruits and oils.
One should pass the time with Cāndrāyaṇa observances or always subsist on Kṛcchra penances; or one may eat once every fortnight, or once every month, or once a day has passed.

Pure, he should sleep on the ground at night; during the day, he should spend his time standing on tiptoe, or by alternating between standing, sitting, and walking, or again by the practice of yoga. (3.51)
In summer he should stand amidst five fires; during the rains, he should sleep on the bare ground;
and in winter, he should wear wet clothes, or else perform penance according to his ability. (3.52)
He who pricks with thorns and he who anoints with sandalwood—toward both of them he is equal, neither angry nor pleased. (3.53)

Or, having internalized the sacred fires within himself, dwelling among trees and eating sparingly, he should beg for alms solely for the sake of sustenance at the dwellings of forest-dwellers. (3.54)
Or, having brought morsels from a village, he should eat eight of them while restraining his speech; or, subsisting on air, he should walk toward the northeast until his body is worn away. (3.55)

Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee, either from the household or from the forest, and having at its conclusion consigned those fires into oneself; ||3.56||

Having studied the Vedas, performed recitations, fathered sons, given food, maintained the sacred fires, and offered sacrifices according to his ability, he should then set his mind on liberation; it cannot be otherwise. (3.57)

Devoted to the welfare of all beings, tranquil, carrying the triple staff and the water-pot, delighting in solitude, he should wander as a mendicant and resort to a village for the sake of alms. (3.58)
Free from attachment, he should wander for alms in the evening, unobserved, in a village devoid of other mendicants, seeking only enough for his sustenance. (3.59)
The vessels of ascetics are made of clay, bamboo, wood, or gourd;
their purification is by water and scrubbing with cow-hair.
Having restrained the collection of senses, having abandoned passion and hatred, and having cast off fear toward living beings, the twice-born attains immortality. (3.61)
However, the purification of one's intention must be performed especially by a mendicant, because it is the cause for the arising of knowledge and for the attainment of independence. (3.62)

One must contemplate dwelling in the womb, as well as the destinies born of karma; likewise, one must contemplate mental afflictions, physical diseases, old age, and the transformation of physical form. (3.63)
Existence through thousands of births, and the reversal of the pleasant and unpleasant—these are to be perceived through the yoga of meditation; the subtle Self is established within the self. (3.64)
The stage of life is not the cause of dharma; for dharma exists when it is being practiced.
Therefore, one should not do to another that which is unwholesome for oneself. (3.65)
Truthfulness, non-stealing, freedom from anger, modesty, purity, wisdom, fortitude, self-restraint, control of the senses, and knowledge—this is declared to be the universal dharma. (3.66)
Just as sparks fly forth from a heated mass of iron, even so do all selves emerge from the Self. (3.67)
In that regard, the self indeed performs some action by itself, some by its own nature, and some through habituation, consisting of merit, demerit, and rebirth. (3.68)
The sign, the syllable, the agent, the knower, Brahman, the possessor of qualities, and the controller—he is unborn, yet he is proclaimed as "born" due to the assumption of a body. (3.69)
Just as at the beginning of creation he emits space, air, fire, water, and earth—
each possessing one additional quality— so too does he take them back while coming into being.
The sun is nourished by the oblation; from that comes rain, and then the plants.
That food, in the form of essence, attains the state of semen. (3.71)
When there is union between a woman and a man, and the semen and blood are pure, the Lord simultaneously takes up the five elements with himself as the sixth. (3.72)
The sense organs, the mind, the vital breath, knowledge, life-span, happiness, fortitude, retention, impulse, suffering, desire, and likewise egoism—these are [the functions of the intellect]. (3.73)
Effort, form, and appearance; the musical notes and their dissonances; existence and non-existence—all this is born of his own self, as he desires a beginning for that which is beginningless. (3.74)
In the first month, it becomes a mass of moisture, a congealing of the elements;
in the second month, it is an *arbuda*; but in the third month, it is endowed with limbs and sense organs. (3.75)
From space [he obtains] lightness, subtlety, sound, the sense of hearing, and likewise strength;
from air, however, impulsion, movement, expansion, and even dryness. (3.76)
Fire, however, has visibility, digestion, heat, and the illumination of form;
from water come taste, coolness, moisture, lubrication, and softness. (3.77)
The self perceives the odor of the earth, as well as the sense of smell, heaviness, and form; therefore, it vibrates in its entirety during the third month. (3.78)
By not granting her pregnancy-longings, the fetus may incur defects, deformity, or even death; therefore, one should do what is pleasing to the woman. (3.79)
In the fourth week, there is stability of the limbs; in the fifth, the production of blood;
and in the sixth, the emergence of strength, complexion, nails, and body hair.
Endowed with mind and consciousness, and pervaded by channels, sinews, and veins,
he possesses skin in the seventh and eighth [stages], as well as memory.
Again his vitality flows away from the embryo and again from the nurse;
therefore, the embryo born in the eighth month is deprived of life.
In the ninth or even the tenth month, by powerful winds of birth,
he is expelled like an arrow through the opening of a machine, accompanied by feverish distress.
His body is composed of six parts, for it is indeed supported by six layers of skin;
likewise, its limbs are six, and its bones number three hundred and sixty.
Together with the sockets, there are sixty-four teeth; the nails are twenty;
and for the digits of the hands and feet, there are four locations for them. (3.85)
There are sixty bones in the fingers; two in the two heels; four in the ankles; four bones in the forearms, and exactly that many in the shanks. (3.86)
One should point out two each produced at the knees, the palms, the thighs, the shoulders, the axle (the spine), the palate, the uvula, and the pelvic bones. (3.87)
There is one bone in the pubic region, as well as forty-five in the back;
there are fifteen bones in the neck, one in each clavicle, and likewise one in the jaw. (3.88)
At its base are two [bones], the frontal bone, the cheekbone, the nasal bone, and the jawbone; together with the ribs and their sockets, and the arbudas, there are seventy-two. (3.89)
There are two temples, four skull-bones, and likewise seventeen bones in the chest; such is the collection of bones in a person. (3.90)
Odor, form, taste, touch, and sound are known as the objects;
the nose, eyes, tongue, skin, and ear are the sense organs. (3.91)
One should know that the hands, the anus, the generative organ, the mouth, and the feet as the fifth are the organs of action; and the mind is of the nature of both. 3.92
The navel, the vital energy (ojas), the rectum, the semen, the blood, the two temples, as well as the head, the heart, and the throat—these are the abodes of the vital breath (prāṇa). 3.93.
The omentum, the instrument for removing the omentum, the navel, the lungs, the liver, the spleen, the small intestine, the two kidneys, the bladder, and the receptacle of feces; 3.94.
The stomach, the heart, the large intestine, the anus, and the abdomen—this is declared to be the extent of the abdominal cavity. (3.95)
The two pupils, the two eye-sockets, the two ear-cavities, the two ears, the two cheeks, the two temples, the two eyebrows, the two gums, the two lips, and the two hollows of the loins. (3.96)
The groins, the testicles, the kidneys, the two masses of phlegm, the breasts, the uvula, the buttocks, the arms, the shanks, and the thighs with their calves; 3.97.
The abdomen, the bladder-head, the chin, the goitre, and the nape of the neck—these are the locations here in this body. (3.98)
The four eyelids, the feet, the hands, and the heart—these nine apertures are indeed the abodes of the vital breath (prāṇa). 3.99
There are exactly seven hundred vessels (sirā), nine hundred sinews (snāyu), two hundred channels (dhamanī), and five hundred muscles (peśī). ||3.100||
Twenty-nine hundred thousand, nine hundred, and fifty-six vessels designated as *dhamanīs* have been specified. (3.101)
The wise should know that there are three hundred thousand hairs on the head and beard;
likewise, there are one hundred and eight vital points (marmas) and two hundred joints.
There are fifty-four crores, sixty-seven hundred thousand, and half a [thousand] pores of the body, together with the openings for sweat. (3.103)
The atoms are distinguished and reckoned by means of the winds;
if they were otherwise, who indeed could know the established nature of these entities? (3.104)
Nine añjalis of rasa are to be known, ten of water, seven of feces, and eight of blood are proclaimed. (3.105)
Phlegm is six [parts], bile five, and urine four;
fat three, and adipose tissue two; marrow one, and half a part in the head. (3.106)
"The vital essence of phlegm is just this much, and the semen is just this much;
thus, this body is unstable—he who acts for the sake of liberation [should realize this]. (3.107)
Seventy-two thousand channels named Hitā issue forth from the heart; in their midst is that which has the luster of the moon.
The mandala has its center in the self, which is as immovable as a lamp;
having known that which is in the center, one is not born again. (3.109)
That which I obtained from Āditya is to be known as the *Āraṇyaka*;
and the *Yogaśāstra* proclaimed by me is to be known by one who desires Yoga. (3.110)
Having made the mind, intellect, memory, and senses focused on no other object, one should meditate upon that Lord who dwells as the Self within the heart like a lamp. (3.111)
Just as a man sings the *sāman* chant without piercing it through proper attentiveness, so too does one attain the supreme Brahman through attentive practice. 3.112
The Aparāntaka, Ullopya, Madraka, Prakarī, as well as Auveṇaka, Sarobindu, and the Uttara Gītikās. (3.113)
The *ṛk*, *gāthā*, *pāṇikā*, *dakṣavihitā*, and *brahmagītikā*—this is what is called "song" (*geya*), so designated because it is produced through the practice of that [chanting]. (3.114)
One who knows the true principles of playing the lute, who is proficient in the musical scales and modes, and who understands the rhythmic cycles, enters the path of yoga without effort. (3.115)
If one who knows the song does not attain the supreme state through yoga, he becomes an attendant of Rudra and rejoices together with him. (3.116)
The self is said to be beginningless, and its beginning is the body;
the entire world arises from the self, and the self originates from the world. (3.117)
"How is it that we, along with the worlds of gods, asuras, and humans, are thus bewildered?
Tell us how the universe arose and how the Self exists within it. (3.118)
When this web of delusion is cast aside, that person is indeed seen,
possessing a thousand hands, feet, and eyes, with the splendor of the sun, appearing in thousands of forms.
He is indeed the Self, the sacrifice, the omniform Prajāpati;
as the Virāj, he assumes the state of the sacrifice in the form of Soma.
That supreme essence which arises from the renunciation of substance and deity,
having fully satisfied the gods, [satisfies] the sacrificer with its fruit.
Having been joined with the wind, the Soma is then led by the rays;
it is brought to the solar abode ordained by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
That sun creates that maṇḍala, the supreme nectar,
from which arises the birth of all beings, whether they are of the nature of eaters or non-eaters.
From that food, again comes sacrifice; from sacrifice, again food; and from food, again ritual action.
Thus does this wheel revolve, without beginning or end. (3.124)
The self is beginningless; no origination exists for the inner self.
But the person is a composite entity, born of delusion, desire, aversion, and karma. (3.125)
That primordial deity whom I have described to you as the thousandfold self— from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet, the social orders (varṇas) were born in their respective order. (3.126)
From his feet the earth was born, and from his head the sky;
from his nose the vital breaths, from his ears the directions, from his skin the wind, and from his mouth the fire.
From his mind the moon was born, and from his eye the sun; from his loins arose the intermediate space and the entire world with its moving and unmoving beings.
If this is so, O Brahmin, how is it that he is born in evil wombs?
How is it that he, who is the Lord, is joined with undesirable states of being? (3.129)

And why does one who possesses the instruments [of cognition] not know their prior cognition? Furthermore, why does one who is omnipresent not feel the sensation [experienced by another], even though he too is omnipresent? (3.130)
Through the defects born of the actions of mind, speech, and body, this living being undergoes the state of being an animal or an immobile thing across hundreds of births. (3.131)
For just as the states of beings within their bodies are infinite, so too are the forms of embodied beings here in all wombs. 3.132

The ripening of karmas for some occurs after death; for others it arises in this life; and for yet others it occurs both here and hereafter—their underlying disposition is the determining factor in each case. (3.133)
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable, and being intent on falsehoods, one is born into the lowest wombs. (3.134)
A man who speaks untruth, a slanderer, and one who indulges in irrelevant chatter is born among beasts and birds. (3.135)

One who delights in taking what is not given, who consorts with the wives of others, and who is a violent injurer of immobile beings by improper means, is reborn among the stationary entities. (3.136)

One who knows the self, who is pure, self-controlled, ascetic, has restrained senses, performs dharma, and is learned in the Vedas—such a person of sattvic nature goes to the wombs of the gods. (3.137)
He who delights in the doctrine that the effect does not pre-exist in the cause, who is unsteady, enterprising, and sensual—he, being of rajasic nature among men, attains birth after death. (3.138)
One who is sleepy, cruel, greedy, an atheist, a beggar, as well as one who is negligent and of broken conduct, being characterized by tamas, shall be born among the animals. (3.139)
Overcome by passion and darkness,
wandering here and joined with undesirable states of being, he enters into the cycle of existence.
For just as a dirty mirror is incapable of reflecting forms, so too the self with its faculties unripened is incapable of knowledge. (3.141)
Just as the sweet taste is not perceived in unripe *kaṭu* and *urvāru* fruits despite its presence, so too knowledge is not attained within the self when the faculties are unripened. (3.142)
An embodied being experiences sensation throughout his entire body;
but the yogi who is disciplined does not experience sensation in any part of it. (3.143)
Just as the single space appears distinct within jars and other vessels, so too the single Self appears manifold, like the sun reflected in various receptacles of water. 3.144
Brahmā, ether, wind, fire, water, and earth are the constituent elements;
these are the worlds, this is the Self, and from that [arises] all that is moving and unmoving. (3.145)
Just as a potter creates a jar through the conjunction of clay, a staff, and a wheel, or as a house-builder constructs a house with grass, clay, and wood; || 3.146 ||
Just as a goldsmith [fashions] a form by taking only gold, or as a silkworm produces a cocoon through the union with its own saliva. ||3.147||
Taking up such causes as these, the Self alone creates itself within those various wombs here, having brought together the instruments of action.
The great elements are real, and the self is likewise; for who, having seen with one eye, could see again with the other? (3.149)
Who indeed understands speech once it has been heard again and again?
Whose is the memory of past objects, and who is the creator of dreams? (3.150)
Proud on account of birth, form, age, conduct, learning, and so forth, he is attached to objects such as sound through action, mind, and speech. (3.151)
With his mind full of doubt as to whether the fruit of karma exists or not, he is overwhelmed;
for even though he is unestablished, he considers himself established. (3.152)
"I have a wife, children, and ministers; I belong to them"—thus I stand, my mind always perverted regarding what is beneficial and what is harmful. (3.153)
He is impartial toward the learned and the ignorant, as well as toward the primordial nature and its transformations; he is intent upon fasting, entering fire, or leaping into water. (3.154)
One who behaves in this way, being undisciplined in self and possessed of false attachments, is bound by action, by hatred and delusion, and indeed by desire. (3.155)
Service to the teacher, discernment of the meaning of the Vedic scriptures, the performance of those prescribed duties, association with the virtuous, and auspicious speech. (3.156)
Avoiding the sight and touch of women, beholding the Self within all beings, renouncing possessions, and wearing worn-out saffron robes. ||3.157||
The restraint of the senses from their objects, the abandonment of sloth and laziness, the thorough examination of the body, and the perception of evil in worldly activities. || 3.158 ||
Freedom from passion and darkness, purity of being, desirelessness, and tranquility—purified by these means, one who is fit for the state of pure being shall become immortal. (3.159)
Through the establishment of mindfulness of reality, through the application of being, through the exhaustion of karmas, and through proximity to the virtuous, the practice of yoga proceeds. (3.160)
He whose mind, established in purity, rests upon the Lord at the dissolution of the body, with his memory unimpaired, shall truly attain the state of remembering past births. (3.161)
Just as Bharata sustains his own body by means of colors,
creating various forms, so too does the Self sustain the body born of karma.
Never at any time has this Self been previously liberated from egoism, from the mind, from the course of rebirth, from the fruit of karma, and from the body. (3.164)
One who is generous, truthful, patient, wise, of virtuous deeds, and has conquered the senses;
one who practices austerity and is devoted to yoga, is not overcome by diseases. (3.165)

Just as the stability of a lamp depends on the combination of the wick, the support, and the oil, so too is its transformation observed; likewise, the destruction of life occurs even before its time. (3.166)
Infinite are his rays, like those of a lamp situated within the heart;
they are white, black, tawny, blue, reddish-brown, yellow, and red. (3.167)
One among them stands above; having pierced the solar orb and transcended the world of Brahmā, by that [path] one goes to the supreme goal. (3.168)
That other hundred rays of his which are situated directly upwards—by means of them, he reaches the abodes of the hosts of gods. (3.169)
Those various rays of his that are below and of gentle luster are for the purpose of experiencing karma; by means of them, he wanders here helplessly. (3.170)
Through the Vedas, the scriptures, and specialized knowledge; through birth and death; through mental distress, departure, and likewise arrival; and indeed through truth and falsehood. (3.171)

Through higher states and through pleasure and pain, by means of actions—both auspicious and inauspicious—and by the knowledge of omens and portents, as well as the results arising from the conjunctions of the planets. ||3.172||
By the movements of the stars and constellations, by those born of water, and even by those born of dreams;
likewise, by space, wind, light, water, earth, and darkness. (3.173)
Even through the passing of Manvantaras and Yugas, or by the power of mantras and medicinal herbs,
one cannot perceive the Self, which is the eternal cause of the world.
Egoity, memory, intelligence, aversion, intellect, happiness, fortitude, the transition between different senses, desire, retention, and life—[these are the functions of the mind]. (3.175)
The creation of objects in dreams, the impelling of the mind, its movement, the blinking of the eyes, consciousness, effort, and the grasping of the five elements; 3.176.
Since these signs of the Supreme Self are perceived, therefore there exists beyond the body the embodied one, the all-pervading Lord. (3.177)
The sense organs together with their objects, the mind, the organs of action, as well as the ego-sense, the intellect, and the elements beginning with earth; 3.178.
The unmanifest Self is declared to be the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) of this field;
it is the Lord of all beings, being both existent and non-existent, as well as both existent and non-existent. (3.179)

The arising of the intellect (buddhi) is from the unmanifest; from that, the emergence of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra); and from that, the elements beginning with space are born, each possessing one additional quality [than its predecessor]. (3.180)
