Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their qualities;
whichever of these is dependent upon a particular element, it dissolves back into that very place. (3.181)
I have told you how the Self creates itself, even though it is the Lord, through the ripening of the three kinds of karma. (3.182)
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are indeed proclaimed to be its very qualities;
for when possessed by rajas and tamas, it revolves like a wheel. (3.183)
This supreme Puruṣa, who is both without beginning and yet possesses a beginning, is declared to be subject to modification when apprehended through the subtle body and the senses. ||3.184||
Between the path of the fathers (pitṛyāna), the path of the non-horses (ajavīthī), and that of Agastya, by that path those who maintain the sacred fire and desire offspring go toward heaven.
Even those who are devoted to generosity and endowed with the eight right qualities, being dedicated to the vow of truth, go by that very same path. (3.186)
Eighty-eight thousand sages who were householders will return again to this world; they are the seeds and the promoters of the Dharma. (3.187)
Between the Seven Sages and the Naga-pathway, there dwell those who have taken refuge in the world of the gods;
they are likewise as many sages, entirely free from all worldly undertakings. (3.188)
By means of austerity, celibacy, renunciation of attachment, and wisdom,
they go there and remain until the dissolution of all beings.
For from it [proceed] the Vedas, the Purāṇas, as well as the sciences and the Upaniṣads;
the verses, the aphorisms, the commentaries, and whatever else constitutes the realm of speech anywhere. (3.190)
The recitation of the Vedas, sacrifice, celibacy, austerity, self-restraint, constant faith, and fasting are the causes for the knowledge of the Self. (3.191)
For he is indeed to be meditated upon by all the stages of life (āśramas) in this very manner;
furthermore, he is to be seen, reflected upon, and heard by the twice-born.
Those twice-born ones who know him thus, and those who have retired to the forest, worship the Truth, endowed with supreme faith. (3.193)
In due order, they pass through the flame, the day, the bright fortnight, and likewise the northern solstice,
the world of the gods, the sun, and that which possesses lightning.
Then a person born of the mind approaches them and makes them inhabitants of the world of Brahmā; for them, there is no return here again. ||3.195||
For those men who have conquered heaven through sacrifice, austerity, and gifts,
[they go] to smoke, then to night, then to the dark fortnight, and likewise to the southern solstice.
The world of the ancestors, the moon, the sky, the wind, the water, and the earth—they arise here in this sequence, and they go back again. 3.197.
He who does not understand these two paths for himself will become either a venomous snake, a moth, an insect, or a worm. (3.198)
With the feet placed supine upon the thighs, one should place the other hand on the left;
slightly raising the face and supporting it with the chest. (3.199)
With eyes closed, established in sattva, not touching tooth against tooth, with the tongue motionless against the palate, the mouth closed, and perfectly steady. (3.200)
Having restrained the collection of the senses and sitting on a seat that is neither too low nor too high, one should undertake breath control (prāṇāyāma) twice or even thrice. (3.201)
Then that Lord who resides in the heart like a lamp should be meditated upon; there the wise one, maintaining concentration, should fix the self. (3.202)
Invisibility, memory, luster, vision, as well as the power of hearing, and likewise the ability to enter another's body after casting off one's own body. (3.203)
The creation of objects at will is indeed the characteristic mark of perfection in yoga;
when yoga is perfected, one who casts off the body becomes fit for immortality. (3.204)

Or again, even one who has renounced ritual action, dwelling with his son while studying the Veda, eating only what is unasked for and being moderate in diet, shall attain the supreme perfection. (3.205)

One who has acquired wealth by righteous means, who is devoted to the knowledge of reality, who is fond of guests, who performs ancestral rites, and who speaks the truth—even such a householder is liberated. (3.206)
Having reached the terrible and censured hells born of great sins (mahāpātaka), those who committed such great sins are reborn here upon the exhaustion of their karma. (3.207)
The killer of a Brahmin goes into the wombs of dogs, pigs, deer, and camels; the drinker of spirituous liquor [goes] into those of donkeys, Pulkasas, and Śvapākas—of this there is no doubt. (3.208)
A stealer of gold shall become a worm, an insect, or a moth;
and one who violates the teacher’s bed shall gradually become grass, a shrub, or a creeper.

The killer of a Brahmin shall suffer from consumption; the drinker of spirituous liquor, from black teeth; the stealer of gold, from deformed nails; and the violator of the Guru’s bed, from skin disease. (3.210)
Whichever of these one drinks from with whom, he is born bearing the characteristics of that person.
A stealer of food shall be afflicted with disease; a non-speaker shall be mute. (3.211)
One who steals grain shall have an extra limb; a slanderer, a putrid nose; one who steals oil, a craving for oil; and a backbiter, a foul-smelling mouth. (3.212)
Having abducted another's wife and having stolen the property of a Brahmin, one is born as a Brahma-rākṣasa in a waterless region of the forest. (3.213)
Those who steal jewels are reborn in a low caste; having stolen leaf-vegetables, one becomes a peacock, and having stolen fine fragrances, one becomes a muskrat. (3.214)
A mouse portends the theft of grain; a camel, a vehicle; a monkey, fruit; a goat, livestock; a crow, milk; and a house-builder, household utensils. (3.215)
A honeybee [destroys] honey, a vulture a piece of meat, a monitor lizard a cow, and a heron likewise fire;
one with white leprosy destroys clothing, a dog destroys broth, and a cricket destroys salt. (3.216)
This has been stated by me merely as an illustration regarding the act of theft;
for just as there are various kinds of property, so too are there various classes of living beings. (3.217)

Having thus experienced the state of an animal in accordance with their karma through the passage of time, they are born as the lowest of men—destitute, lacking auspicious marks, and impoverished. (3.218)
Then, having become free from blemish, they are born into great families as enjoyers of wealth, endowed with auspicious marks, and possessed of riches and grain. (3.219)
By failing to perform what is prescribed, by engaging in what is censured, and by not restraining the senses, a person undergoes a fall. (3.220)
Therefore, he must perform an expiation here for the sake of purification;
in this way, both his inner self and the world will be appeased. (3.221)
Sin committed through ignorance is removed by penances;
however, one who acts intentionally becomes fit for social intercourse here only by virtue of a scriptural declaration. (3.222)
Men who do not perform penance for their sins, being devoted to wickedness and devoid of remorse, go to terrible and agonizing hells. (3.223)
Tāmisra, Lohaśaṅku, Mahāniraya, Śalmalī, Raurava, Kuḍmala, Pūtimṛttika, and Kālasūtraka. (3.224)
Saṃghāta, Lohitoda, Saviṣa, Saṃpratāpana, the great Naraka Kākola, Saṃjīvana, and Nadīpatha. (3.225)
Avīci, Andhatāmisra, and likewise Kumbhīpāka; Asipatravana and Tapana, making twenty-one in total.

Worst among men, who have not performed expiation, go [to hell] accompanied by the terrible sins born of the great transgressions (mahāpātaka) as well as those born of the minor transgressions (upapātaka). (3.227)

The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, and likewise the violator of the Guru’s bed—these are the perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin), as is he who drinks with them for a year. (3.228)
Excessive reviling of gurus, disparaging the Vedas, and the killing of a friend—these are indeed equal to the murder of a Brahmin, as is the destruction of what has been studied. (3.229)
Eating what is forbidden, dishonesty, speaking falsehood for the sake of self-exaltation, and tasting the mouth of a woman in her menses are equal to the drinking of liquor. (3.230)
The theft of a horse, a jewel, a human being, a woman, land, or a milch cow, as well as the misappropriation of a deposit, is indeed equal to the theft of gold. (3.231)

They consider sexual intercourse with the wives of friends, virgins, women of one's own uterine kin, women of the lowest castes, women of the same lineage, and the wives of sons to be equivalent to violating the Guru’s bed. (3.232)

The father’s sister, the maternal uncle’s wife, the daughter-in-law, the mother’s sister, as well as the mother’s co-wife, a sister, and likewise the teacher’s daughter—[one should not approach these]. (3.233)

But he who approaches the wife of his teacher or his own daughter is a violator of the guru’s bed; his penis shall be cut off and he shall be put to death, as shall the woman if she was willing. (3.234)
Killing a cow, being a *vrātya*, theft, non-payment of debts, failing to maintain the sacred fires, selling forbidden goods, and marrying before an elder brother; 3.235.
Receiving instruction for a fee, teaching for a fee, adultery, a younger brother marrying before his elder, usury, and the manufacture of salt; 3.236.
Killing a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; living by means of censured wealth;
atheism; the neglect of religious vows; and the sale of one's own sons. (3.237)
Stealing grain, silver, or cattle; officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice; abandoning one's father, mother, or friend; and the sale of a pond or a garden. (3.238)

Violating a maiden, officiating at the sacrifice of one who has married before his elder brother, giving a daughter in marriage to such a man, and crookedness—these constitute the loss of Brahmanhood. (3.239)
Engaging in ritual acts for one's own sake, consorting with women who drink liquor, abandoning one's private Vedic study, the sacred fires, and one's sons, as well as abandoning one's kinsmen; 3.240.
Cutting down trees for the sake of firewood, living by the slaughter of women or by medicinal herbs, the construction of murderous machines, and the sale of oneself—these are vices. (3.241)
Studying false scriptures, officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy of the sacred sources, and the selling of one's wife—each of these is a minor offense (upapātaka). (3.242)
Carrying a skull as his banner, subsisting on alms, and making his deed known, the slayer of a Brahmin shall attain purification after twelve years by eating sparingly. (3.243)
Or indeed, one may offer the body, beginning with the hair and ending with the marrow, with these mantras in their proper sequence, saying: "Svāhā to the hairs! and so forth. (3.244)
One may attain purification by rescuing a Brāhmaṇa, or by saving twelve cows, or likewise by performing the final purificatory bath of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. ||3.245||
Having seen on the road a Brahmin or even a cow afflicted by a long-lasting and severe illness, the slayer of a Brahmin becomes pure by restoring them to health. (3.246)
If he has been brought back after all his wealth was stolen, or if he has been killed, or even if he is still alive but wounded by weapons on that account, he is purified. (3.247)
Or, being self-restrained, he may recite the Vedic Saṃhitā three times in the forest;
or, eating moderately, he may purify himself by going against the current of the Sarasvatī river.
Or, being slain in battle as a target, he shall attain purification;
even while living, if he is nearly dead and afflicted by wounds, he is purified. (3.249)
By giving sufficient wealth into the vessel, one attains purification;
and for the sake of the recipient's purification, the Vaiśvānara sacrifice is prescribed. (3.250)
Upon killing a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice, one should perform the vow prescribed for a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa;
likewise for a destroyer of an embryo according to its caste, and for a murderer of an Ātreyī woman. (3.251)

One should observe the vow even if one does not kill, provided one has come together for the purpose of killing; however, if a Brāhmaṇa engaged in a sacrifice is killed, one should observe the vow for double the duration.
Having drunk any one of these—liquor, water, clarified butter, cow’s urine, or milk—that resembles fire in its effect, the drinker of liquor attains purification through death. (3.253)
Either clothed in hair or with matted locks, he should perform the vow for the slayer of a Brahmin;
or he should eat oil-cake or grain-husks at night for one year. (3.254)
But having drunk liquor, or [eaten] semen, feces, or urine through ignorance, the three castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite again; of this there is no doubt. (3.255)
That brahmin woman who drinks liquor does not go to the world of Brahmā;
right here she is reborn as a female dog, a vulture, or a sow. (3.256)
But a Brāhmaṇa who has stolen gold must offer a mace to the king, proclaiming his own deed; whether slain by it or released, he is purified. (3.257)
Without confessing it to the king, one should perform the vow for wine-drinkers for the sake of purification;
or one should give gold equal to one's own weight, or do what brings satisfaction to a Brahmin.
He shall lie upon a heated iron bed with an iron woman;
having had his testicles cut off and seized, he shall cast away his body in the south-western direction.
One who has violated the Guru’s bed shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year,
or the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months while repeatedly reciting the Vedic Saṃhitā.
But he who indeed drinks [the water] together with these for a year becomes equal to them;
he may marry a maiden from among them who is fasting and possesses nothing.
Having killed all types of low-born animals, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
even a Śūdra, though lacking the right to such rites, is purified by this very method over time. (3.262)
The fault of one who brings a false accusation is twice as great as that of one who speaks the truth;
furthermore, by speaking falsely, he takes upon himself the sin of the one who has been falsely accused. (3.263)
A cow-killer, drinking the five products of the cow, shall remain self-restrained for a month;
sleeping in a cow-pen and following the cows, he is purified by the gift of a cow. (3.264)
Or, being composed in mind, he should perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances;
or, having fasted for three nights, he should give ten cows and one bull as a gift.
Purification for a minor offense (upapātaka) may likewise be achieved by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, or by subsisting on milk for a month, or again by the Parāka penance. || 3.266 ||
For killing a Kṣatriya, a man should give a thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh, or else he should perform the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa for three years. (3.267)
A killer of a Vaiśya should perform this for one year or give one hundred cows;
a killer of a Śūdra, however, should do so for six months or give ten milch-cows.

For killing a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or a woman who has behaved wickedly, one should give, respectively, for the sake of purification, a leather water-bag, a bow, a goat, or a sheep. (3.269)
Having killed a woman who is not corrupt, one should perform the vow for killing a Śūdra;
likewise for a thousand vertebrate animals, or a cartload of those without bones.
Having killed a cat, an iguana, a mongoose, a frog, a dog, or a bird, one should drink milk for three days or perform a quarter-kṛcchra penance.
For an elephant, five blue bulls; for a parrot, a two-year-old calf; for a donkey, a goat, or a sheep, a bull should be given; and for a crane, a three-year-old [bull]. (3.272)

Having killed a hawk, a monkey, a carnivorous beast, or a water-bird such as a peacock, and having killed a vulture, one should give a cow; however, among non-carnivorous animals, one should give a heifer.
For killing snakes, an iron rod must be given; for a eunuch, a māṣaka of tin; for a boar, a jar of ghee; for a camel, a guñjā seed; and for a horse, a piece of fine cloth. (3.274)
But one who is unable to give a drona of sesame seeds for each partridge, or for elephants and other such beings, shall perform a kṛcchra penance for the purification of each individual. (3.275)
Something must be given when killing a creature with bones; however, for one without bones, there should be a breath-restraint (prāṇāyāma).
For cutting down trees, shrubs, creepers, or climbing plants, one hundred Ṛg-verses should be recited.
One who has been bitten by an unchaste woman, a monkey, a donkey, a dog,
or a crow is purified by performing breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) in water and consuming clarified butter.
Upon killing a living being produced from fruit, flowers, food, or sap, one should subsist on ghee;
for the useless cutting of medicinal herbs, one should subsist on milk and follow cows for a day.

Having consecrated the spilled semen with these two verses, "yan me 'dya retaḥ" and so forth, one should touch the space between the breasts or the eyebrows with that [semen] using the ring finger. ||3.279||
Having seen one's own reflection in water, one should mutter "Maya tejaḥ";
likewise, when one has seen something impure, or when there is fickleness, or even in the case of falsehood, one should mutter the Gāyatrī.
A student of sacred knowledge who, having gone to a woman, becomes an *avakīrṇin*, is purified by sacrificing an ass as an animal offering to Nirṛti. (3.281)

But having neglected the begging for alms and the fire-ritual for seven nights while not being ill, one should offer two oblations of clarified butter with these two [verses] beginning with "kāmāvakīrṇaḥ. (3.282)
Then one should perform the ritual attendance with the mantra "saṃ mā siñca";
for eating honey or meat, a *kṛcchra* penance must be performed, as well as the remaining vows. (3.283)
If one sent on a mission should die, the preceptor should perform three *kṛcchra* penances;
having acted contrary to the will of the preceptor, one becomes pure by propitiating him. (3.284)

If a Brahmin dies while receiving assistance through the administration of medicines, food, and the like, or through medical treatments and other therapeutic procedures, there is no sin; nor is there sin when cattle, bulls, and others die during the ripening [of crops] or during the application of medicinal remedies and fire-rituals. (3.285)
He who falsely accuses another of a great sin or a minor sin should subsist on water for one month, reciting [mantras] with his senses restrained. (3.286)

One who has been falsely accused should perform the arduous penance (kṛcchra) prescribed for fire, or he should offer a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) to Vāyu, or even an animal sacrifice to Vāyu. (3.287)
One who approaches his brother's wife without being authorized should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
by approaching a woman in her courses, he becomes purified after consuming clarified butter at the end of three nights. (3.288)
A student living in a cow-pen for one month, subsisting on milk alone and devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī, is liberated from the sin of accepting improper gifts. (3.289)
One who performs sacrifices for those unworthy of them (vrātyas), even if performing malevolent rites, shall perform three kṛcchra penances;
likewise one who has forgotten the Veda, one who has abandoned a person seeking refuge, shall subsist on barley for a year.
Having bathed, one should perform breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) after riding in a vehicle drawn by a donkey or a camel;
likewise, after bathing naked, sleeping naked, or having sexual intercourse with a woman during the day.
Having addressed a guru as "thou," or having uttered "huṃ" to him, or having defeated a Brahmin in debate, or having struck or bound one, he shall immediately appease him and fast for a day. (3.292)
If one raises a weapon to strike another, the penance is a *kṛcchra*; if one actually strikes him down, it is an *atikṛcchra*;
if blood flows, it is a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*; and if the blood is internal, it is a *kṛcchra*. (3.293)
Having carefully considered the place, the time, the age, the capacity, and the nature of the sin, an expiation should be prescribed where no specific atonement has been mentioned. (3.294)
His own kinsmen should pour out a water-pot filled with water through a female slave;
they should exclude him from all ritual activities as one who has fallen. (3.295)
When he has returned having fulfilled his vow, they should offer him a new water-jar;
they should not despise him, and they should drink from it together with him in every respect.
This same rule is proclaimed for women who have become outcasts:
they should be given a dwelling near the house, along with food, clothing, and protection. (3.297)
Approaching a low-caste man, causing an abortion, and harming one's husband—these also certainly constitute specific acts leading to the loss of caste for women. (3.298)

One should not associate with those who harm those who have sought refuge, children, or women, nor with these: even if they have fulfilled their vows, they are ungrateful; one must avoid such as these. (3.299)
When the funeral vessel has been set aside, one standing in the midst of the kinsmen should first give fodder to the cows; this is the joint rite for one who has been honored by the cows. (3.300)
One whose fault is publicly known should perform a vow approved by an assembly;
however, one whose fault is not publicly known should practice a secret vow. (3.301)
Having fasted for three nights and recited the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn while submerged in water, even a killer of a Brahmin is purified by giving a milch cow. 3.302.
For indeed, having slept in the water during the day, the wind-eater should offer forty oblations of clarified butter, saying, "Svāhā to the body hairs! (3.303).
Having fasted for three nights and offered clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍī verses, one becomes pure;
but the drinker of spirituous liquor or the stealer of gold, standing in water, must recite the Rudra hymns.
One who has violated the Guru’s bed is purified by reciting the *Sahasraśīrṣa* [hymn] a thousand times;
at the conclusion of the rite, a milch cow must be given separately for each of these acts.
One should perform a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) for the removal of all sins, as well as for those arising from minor offenses (upapātaka) and for those not specifically mentioned. (3.306)
A twice-born man who has consumed semen, feces, or urine after having observed the preparatory fast (upavāsa) shall drink the purifying Soma-liquid consecrated with the syllable Oṃ. (3.307)
Whatever sin has been committed through ignorance, whether by night or by day, all of that perishes by performing the twilight devotions at the three periods of the day. (3.308)
The recitation of the Śukriya Āraṇyaka and the Gāyatrī mantra a thousand times is declared to remove all sins, as is the Rudraikādaśinī.
And wherever a twice-born man considers himself defiled, there he should perform an oblation with sesame seeds or simply recite the Sāvitrī mantra. (3.310)
Sins, even those born of the great transgressions, do not touch one who is devoted to the study of the Vedas, who is patient, and who delights in the performance of the five sacrifices. (3.311)

Subsisting on air, standing during the day and spending the night in water while gazing at the sun, and having recited the Gāyatrī a thousand times, one is purified—except for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. (3.312)
Celibacy, compassion, patience, meditation, truthfulness, sincerity, non-violence, non-stealing, freedom from malice, and self-restraint—these are recorded as the *yamas*. (3.313)
Bathing, silence, fasting, sacrifice, study of the Vedas, restraint of the generative organ, service to the teacher, purity, freedom from anger, and generosity are the observances (niyamas). (3.314)
Having drunk the five products of the cow—cow’s milk, curd, urine, dung, and ghee—one should fast on the following day while performing the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance. (3.315)
With each of the various *sāntapana* substances taken on six days, followed by a day of fasting, this seven-day rite is known as the *mahāsāntapana* penance. (3.316)

The *parṇakṛcchra* is declared to consist of the daily practice, performed individually, of water infused with leaves of the *parṇa*, *udumbara*, *rājīva*, and *bilva* trees, along with *kuśa* grass. (3.317)
One should drink hot milk, hot ghee, and hot water, each for one day respectively, followed by a fast for one night; this is declared to be the *taptakṛcchra* penance. (3.318)
By eating once a day, by eating only at night, likewise by eating only what is unasked for,
and by one fast, the Pādakṛcchra is proclaimed.
In whatever manner it may be performed, this threefold penance is called the Prājāpatya;
this very same penance becomes an Atikṛcchra for one who eats only as much food as fills the palm of the hand.
The *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* consists of subsisting on milk for twenty-one days;
the *parāka* is proclaimed to consist of fasting for twelve days. ||3.321||
Taking one of each—oil-cake, water from boiled rice, buttermilk, water, and barley meal—daily, along with one day of fasting, is called the *saumya-kṛcchra*. (3.322)
Through the practice of each of these for three nights in successive order, this is to be known as the "tulāpuruṣa" (weighing against a man), lasting fifteen days. (3.323)

One performing the Cāndrāyaṇa vow should eat as many morsels as there are lunar days in the bright fortnight, with each morsel being the size of a peacock's egg; in the dark fortnight, one should decrease the morsels by one each day.
In whatever manner possible, one should consume exactly two hundred and forty morsels of food within a single month; this is another form of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (3.325)
One who bathes at the three sessions of the day should likewise perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances;
one should recite purificatory mantras and consecrate the funeral cake (piṇḍa) with the Gāyatrī mantra.
Purification for unspecified sins is achieved through the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
he who performs this for the sake of dharma attains the same world as the Moon. (3.327)
One who performs the *kṛcchra* penance while desiring righteousness attains great prosperity;
and just as the fruit of a sacrifice corresponds to its weight, he obtains it without a doubt. (3.328)
Having heard these duties spoken by Yājñavalkya, the high-souled sages spoke thus to the lord of yogis, who possessed immeasurable splendor: [3.329]
Those who, unwearied, shall uphold this treatise on Dharma will attain renown in this world and go to the third heaven.
A seeker of knowledge shall obtain knowledge, and one desiring wealth shall obtain riches;
likewise, one desiring long life shall obtain long life, and one desiring prosperity shall obtain great prosperity. (3.331)
For whoever shall cause even these three verses to be heard at a *śrāddha* ceremony, there will be an infinite satisfaction for the ancestors; of this there is no doubt. (3.332)
Through the retention of this scripture, a Brāhmaṇa attains the state of being a worthy recipient, a Kṣatriya becomes victorious, and a Vaiśya becomes possessed of grain and wealth. (3.333)
If a twice-born man, self-restrained, should cause this to be heard by Brahmins on the sacred festival days (parvan), let your majesty grant him the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. 3.334.
Having heard this speech of the sages, Yājñavalkya, with a joyful soul, said,
"So be it," after bowing down to the Self-existent One.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Expiation," in the Dharmaśāstra of Yājñavalkya.
